language.name: Node.js
language.description: JavaScript on the server. Covers the runtime and event loop, modules and npm, streams, Express and REST APIs, authentication and security, testing, scaling and deployment.

questions.question: What is Node.js, and what does "non-blocking I/O" mean?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Node.js is a runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser, built on Google's V8 engine. Non-blocking I/O means slow work such as reading files or querying a database does not stop the program; Node starts it and keeps serving other requests until the result arrives.

How it works: Node gives JavaScript access to files, the network and processes through built-in modules (fs, http, net). When you call one of these async APIs, the work is handed to the operating system or a background thread, and a callback is queued when it finishes. The single JavaScript thread is never left waiting.

Example: A server that reads a 50 ms database query for each user can still accept new users during those 50 ms, because the thread is free while the query runs.

Common mistake: Calling Node a framework or a language. It is a runtime; Express and NestJS are frameworks that run on it.

Interview tip: Define it in one line (runtime + V8 + non-blocking I/O), then say what it is good at: I/O-heavy APIs and real-time apps.

questions.question: How is JavaScript in Node.js different from JavaScript in the browser?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It is the same language in a different environment. Node has no DOM or window, but it has file, network and process APIs and full access to the operating system.

How it works: Browser globals: window, document, localStorage, fetch. Node globals: process, Buffer, require (CommonJS), __dirname; fetch is built in since Node 18. In Node you choose the version, so you can use modern syntax freely. The security model is also different: browser code is sandboxed, Node code can read and delete files.

Example: A script that uses document.querySelector works in the browser but throws ReferenceError in Node. A script that uses fs.readFile works in Node but not in the browser.

Common mistake: Copying frontend code that touches window or localStorage into a Node script, or putting secrets in frontend code thinking it runs on a server.

Interview tip: Mention that both share the event-loop model, so async concepts (promises, callbacks) carry over.

questions.question: What are V8 and libuv, and what does each one do in Node.js?
questions.answer:
Short answer: V8 runs your JavaScript. libuv is the C library that gives Node its event loop, asynchronous I/O and thread pool.

How it works: V8 parses and compiles JavaScript to machine code, runs it and manages memory with garbage collection. libuv talks to the operating system: it watches sockets with epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS) or IOCP (Windows), runs timers, and uses a small thread pool for work the OS cannot do asynchronously, such as most file operations. Node's C++ bindings connect the two.

Example: fs.readFile('data.txt', cb): V8 runs your call, the binding asks libuv to read the file on a pool thread, and when it finishes libuv queues cb, which V8 then runs on the main thread.

Common mistake: Saying "Node is multi-threaded" or "Node is single-threaded" without nuance. Your JavaScript is single-threaded; libuv uses extra threads behind the scenes.

Interview tip: Draw the chain: JavaScript (V8) -> Node bindings (C++) -> libuv -> operating system.

questions.question: If Node.js is single-threaded, how can it handle 10,000 requests at the same time?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but Node does not wait for slow work. Database, network and file operations are handed to the operating system, and the thread serves other requests in the meantime.

How it works: Most of a request's time is waiting, not computing. Node asks the OS (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) to watch thousands of sockets without one thread per connection. When a result is ready, its callback is queued and the event loop runs it. A thread-per-request server would need 10,000 threads and several GB of memory for the same work.

Example: A route awaits a MongoDB query for 50 ms. During those 50 ms the same thread starts hundreds of other requests, each costing only a little memory.

Common mistake: Thinking Node is good at everything in parallel. If one request does heavy CPU work (resizing images, bcrypt.hashSync, a huge loop), the single thread is busy and every other request waits.

Interview tip: Finish with the limit and the fix: "Great for I/O-heavy work; for CPU-heavy work I would use worker threads, or cluster to use all cores."

questions.question: When should you not choose Node.js for a project?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Avoid Node for long, CPU-heavy work done on the main thread, such as video encoding, large image processing or heavy number crunching.

How it works: CPU work blocks the single JavaScript thread, so every other user waits. Node can still run such work through worker threads, child processes or a job queue, but languages like Go, Rust or Java, or Python with native libraries, are often a better fit for CPU-bound services. Node shines for APIs, real-time apps (chat, live dashboards), streaming, proxies and developer tooling.

Example: A photo-sharing app can use Node for its API and uploads, but send image resizing to a worker pool or a separate service so the API stays fast.

Common mistake: Rejecting Node for anything "big". Large companies run Node at scale; the question is the type of work, not the size of the app.

Interview tip: Show judgement: name a good fit, a bad fit and how you would split the work.

questions.question: What is the process object, and what do you use it for?
questions.answer:
Short answer: process is a global object that describes and controls the running Node process: its environment, arguments, memory and lifecycle.

How it works: Common uses:
process.env: configuration such as PORT and secrets
process.argv: command-line arguments
process.cwd(): the folder Node was started from
process.memoryUsage(): heap and RSS memory
process.on('SIGTERM'): graceful shutdown
process.exitCode: set the exit code without stopping at once

Example: A server reads its port with Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000, and on SIGTERM closes the server and the database before exiting.

Common mistake: Calling process.exit() right after logging or writing a response. It stops immediately, so the log line or the response may never be written. Set process.exitCode and let Node finish instead.

Interview tip: Mention that process is also an EventEmitter (signals, uncaughtException, unhandledRejection).

questions.question: What is the libuv thread pool, and which operations use it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It is a pool of 4 threads (by default) that libuv uses for work the operating system cannot do asynchronously.

How it works: Users of the pool: most fs functions, dns.lookup, async crypto (pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes, randomFill) and zlib compression. Network sockets do not use it, because the OS can watch them asynchronously. The size can be changed with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable (up to 1024), but it must be set before the pool is first used.

Example: During a login spike, 50 users log in at once and each login runs async bcrypt or pbkdf2. Only 4 run at a time; the rest queue, so logins take seconds even though CPU looks fine. Raising the pool to the number of cores, or limiting concurrency, fixes it.

Common mistake: Setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in the middle of the app after a file or crypto call has already started the pool; it has no effect then.

Interview tip: Interviewers like the follow-up "which operations?" Naming fs, dns.lookup, crypto and zlib (and saying sockets do not use it) shows real understanding.

questions.question: What happens step by step when a Node.js server receives an HTTP request?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The OS accepts the connection, libuv notices data on the socket, Node parses the HTTP headers and emits a 'request' event that runs your handler on the main thread.

How it works: 1) The OS completes the TCP handshake. 2) In the poll phase, libuv sees the socket is readable. 3) Node's HTTP parser (llhttp) reads the request line and headers. 4) The server emits 'request' with req (a readable stream for the body) and res (a writable stream). 5) Your handler runs; every await hands the thread back while waiting. 6) res.end() writes the response into the socket, and keep-alive keeps the connection open for the next request.

Example: In Express, app.get('/users') is just a function called in step 5. Body parsers such as express.json() read the req stream before your handler sees req.body.

Common mistake: Thinking the whole body has arrived when the handler starts. For large uploads, req is still streaming; reading it is your job (or a middleware's).

Interview tip: Mentioning that req and res are streams is a strong signal that you understand Node beyond Express.

questions.question: What does "blocking the event loop" mean? Give real examples from APIs.
questions.answer:
Short answer: It means synchronous work runs long enough that no other callback can run, so every request waits behind it.

How it works: Real causes:
Huge JSON: JSON.parse or JSON.stringify on many MB
Sync APIs in routes: fs.readFileSync, bcrypt.hashSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync
Heavy loops: sorting or filtering a million items
Regex on user input: a badly written pattern (ReDoS) can take seconds
The symptom is that all endpoints slow down together and health checks time out.

Example: An export route builds a 200 MB JSON string for a CSV download. While it runs, login and every other route freeze for several seconds.

Common mistake: Moving the work into an async function and expecting it to stop blocking. async does not create a thread; the CPU work still runs on the main thread.

Interview tip: Name how you would detect it: event loop delay with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay, then a CPU profile to find the function.

questions.question: Why do __dirname and __filename not work in ES modules, and what do you use instead?
questions.answer:
Short answer: They exist only in CommonJS. In ES modules, use import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename (Node 20.11+), or build them from import.meta.url.

How it works: CommonJS wraps every file in a function that receives exports, require, module, __filename and __dirname, which is why they look like globals. ES modules have no such wrapper, so those names are undefined and throw ReferenceError. import.meta is the ESM way to get information about the current module.

Example: A route that serves files from a public folder next to the code builds the path with path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'public').

Common mistake: Using process.cwd() instead. It is the folder Node was started from, which changes if you run the app from another folder, so file paths break in production.

Interview tip: Explaining the CommonJS module wrapper is the part that impresses; it also explains why exports, require and module are available.

questions.question: What happens from the moment a browser sends an HTTP request until your Express route sends the response?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The browser finds the server (DNS), opens a TCP connection (plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS) and sends the request. Node's http server parses it and hands it to Express, which runs your middleware in order, matches a route, runs the handler, and the handler writes the response back on the same connection.

How it works:
DNS: the domain becomes an IP address
TCP + TLS: a connection is opened and encrypted (HTTPS)
Node http server: parses the method, URL, headers and body stream, then emits "request"
Express: runs app.use() middleware in order (cors, express.json, auth, validation)
Route handler: does the work (database, other services) without blocking the event loop
Response: res.json() sets headers and the body; the connection stays open (keep-alive) for the next request

Example: POST /api/auth/login: cors() adds headers, express.json() parses the body, a rate limiter counts the attempt, validation checks the email, the controller finds the user in MongoDB, compares the password and returns a JWT with res.json().

Common mistake: A handler that neither sends a response nor calls next(err). The request hangs until the client times out.

Interview tip: Mention where things can go wrong at each step (DNS, TLS, CORS, a slow query) and how you would debug them with the browser Network tab and server logs.

questions.question: Which JavaScript engine does Node.js use?
questions.answer:
Why B: Node is built on Google's V8, the same engine as Chrome.

Why not A: SpiderMonkey is Firefox's engine.

Why not C: JavaScriptCore is Safari's engine (Bun uses it).

Why not D: Chakra was the engine of old Microsoft Edge; a Node fork used it once, but standard Node never did.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT available in Node.js by default?
questions.answer:
Why C: document is part of the browser DOM. There is no page in Node, so it does not exist.

Why not A: process is a Node global for env, argv, signals and more.

Why not B: Buffer is a Node global for binary data.

Why not D: setImmediate is a Node timer that runs in the check phase.

questions.question: Your login route calls bcrypt.hashSync() on every request. What happens under heavy traffic?
options: Node moves the hashing to another thread automatically
Only the login requests slow down
Every request slows down because the main thread is busy hashing
questions.correctAnswer: Every request slows down because the main thread is busy hashing
questions.answer:
Why C: hashSync runs on the main thread. While it hashes (100 ms or more at cost 12), no other callback can run, so every route waits, not only login.

Why not A: Only the async bcrypt.hash() uses the thread pool. The Sync version stays on the main thread.

Why not B: All routes share the one main thread, so they all wait behind the hashing.

Why not D: bcrypt is slow on purpose, to make password guessing expensive.

Fix: Use await bcrypt.hash(password, 12).

questions.question: What is the default size of the libuv thread pool?
questions.answer:
Why B: libuv starts 4 threads unless UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is set before the pool is first used.

Why not A: One thread would make every file and crypto call wait in line.

Why not C and D: Not the default. You can choose 8 or the core count yourself with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.

questions.question: Which of these operations does NOT use the libuv thread pool?
options: Reading data from a TCP socket
questions.correctAnswer: Reading data from a TCP socket
questions.answer:
Why D: Network sockets use the operating system's own async mechanisms (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), so no pool thread is needed.

Why not A: Most fs functions run on pool threads because file I/O is not async on every OS.

Why not B: Async crypto like pbkdf2 is CPU work done on a pool thread.

Why not C: Async zlib compression also runs on the pool.

questions.question: In an ES module on modern Node, how do you get the folder of the current file?
questions.answer:
Why B: import.meta.dirname (Node 20.11+) gives the folder of the current module file.

Why not A: __dirname only exists in CommonJS; in ESM it throws ReferenceError.

Why not C: process.cwd() is where Node was started, which is often a different folder.

Why not D: require does not exist in ES modules.

questions.question: What is the event loop in Node.js?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It is the loop that keeps a Node process running and decides which callback runs next.

How it works: When an async operation finishes (a timer fires, a file is read, a request arrives), its callback is queued. Whenever the call stack is empty, the event loop takes the next callback and runs it. When nothing is left to wait for (no timers, sockets or pending work), the loop ends and the process exits.

Example: A script with setTimeout(fn, 100) stays alive for 100 ms, runs fn, then exits. A server stays alive forever because its listening socket is always pending.

Common mistake: Thinking callbacks run in parallel. They run one at a time on the main thread; only the waiting happens in parallel.

Interview tip: Explain it in three steps: start async work, queue the callback, run it when the stack is empty.

questions.question: What are the phases of the Node.js event loop, in order?
questions.answer:
Short answer: timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, close callbacks; then the loop repeats.

How it works:
timers: setTimeout and setInterval callbacks that are due
pending callbacks: some deferred system errors
idle/prepare: internal use
poll: wait for and run I/O callbacks (most of your code)
check: setImmediate callbacks
close callbacks: such as socket.on('close')
After every single callback, Node empties the process.nextTick queue and then the promise microtask queue.

Example: A file read finishes: its callback runs in poll; a setImmediate scheduled inside it runs in check right after; a setTimeout scheduled inside it waits for the next timers phase.

Common mistake: Saying promises run in a phase. Microtasks are not a phase; they run between callbacks.

Interview tip: If you remember only one thing, remember: poll -> check -> timers, with nextTick and promises in between every callback.

questions.question: What is the difference between process.nextTick and setImmediate?
questions.answer:
Short answer: process.nextTick runs right after the current operation, before promises and before the event loop moves on. setImmediate runs on the next turn of the loop, in the check phase.

How it works: After every callback, Node first empties the nextTick queue, then the promise queue, and only then continues to the next phase. setImmediate callbacks wait in the check phase, which comes right after I/O (poll). So nextTick is 'as soon as possible', setImmediate is 'after pending I/O'.

Example: A library wants to emit an event right after its constructor returns, so listeners added on the next line still receive it; that is a nextTick use. To split a long job into chunks so requests can be served in between, use setImmediate.

Common mistake: Calling nextTick recursively. The queue never empties, I/O never runs and the server freezes.

Interview tip: Say "the names are backwards", then give the order: sync code, nextTick, promises, next phase.

questions.question: In which order do setTimeout(fn, 0) and setImmediate(fn) run?
questions.answer:
Short answer: In the main module the order is not guaranteed. Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs first.

How it works: setTimeout(fn, 0) really means at least 1 ms. When the main module finishes, the loop starts at the timers phase; whether 1 ms has passed depends on how busy the machine is, so either can come first. Inside an I/O callback you are already in the poll phase, and check (setImmediate) comes before the loop wraps around to timers.

Example: Code that schedules work after reading a file with fs.readFile will always see setImmediate before setTimeout 0.

Common mistake: Writing code (or tests) that depends on the main-module order. It can pass on your laptop and fail on a slower server.

Interview tip: Interviewers ask this to see if you answer "it depends" and can explain why.

questions.question: How do you use callback-style Node APIs with async/await?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use Node's built-in promise versions where they exist, util.promisify for other error-first callbacks, and events.once to wait for a single event.

How it works: Promise versions: node:fs/promises, node:timers/promises (setTimeout, setImmediate), node:stream/promises (pipeline, finished), node:dns/promises. util.promisify(fn) turns any (err, result) callback function into one that returns a promise. events.once(emitter, 'name') returns a promise for the next event.

Example: A startup script waits for the server to listen with await once(server, 'listening') and sleeps between retries with await setTimeout(1000) from timers/promises.

Common mistake: Wrapping promise-based APIs in new Promise again, or forgetting that promisify only works with the (err, result) pattern.

Interview tip: Mentioning node:timers/promises and events.once shows you know modern Node, not only util.promisify.

questions.question: What is the error-first callback pattern in Node.js?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Older Node APIs call the callback with the error as the first argument (null if there was none) and the result after it.

How it works: Because an async error cannot be caught with try/catch around the call (the callback runs later), Node passes it as an argument instead. Every callback must check err first and stop if it is set.

Example: fs.readFile('config.json', (err, text) => ...) gets an ENOENT error object as err if the file is missing, and text is undefined.

Common mistake: Forgetting to return after handling the error, so the code continues and crashes on the undefined result. Another one: throwing inside the callback, which nothing can catch.

Interview tip: Mention that util.promisify depends on exactly this pattern.

questions.question: How can process.nextTick starve the event loop?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The nextTick queue is fully emptied before Node continues the loop, so code that keeps adding nextTick callbacks stops I/O, timers and requests from ever running.

How it works: After each callback, Node runs every queued nextTick callback, including ones added while it is emptying the queue. A recursive nextTick therefore never lets the loop reach the poll phase. The same is true for endless promise microtasks. setImmediate does not have this problem because callbacks added during the check phase wait for the next turn.

Example: A queue processor that calls process.nextTick(processNext) for each item looks async, but with a long queue the server stops answering until the queue is empty.

Common mistake: Using nextTick to "yield" in long jobs. It does the opposite of yielding.

Interview tip: Say clearly: nextTick and microtasks never yield to I/O; setImmediate does.

questions.question: You must process 1 million records without freezing the API. How?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Do not run it as one synchronous loop. Process it in chunks that yield to the event loop, stream it, move it to a worker thread, or push it to a background job queue.

How it works:
Chunks: handle 1,000 records, then await setImmediate so requests can run in between.
Streams: read records piece by piece, so memory and CPU stay steady.
Worker thread: run the CPU work in parallel without touching the main thread.
Job queue: for anything longer than a few seconds, add a job (BullMQ with Redis), return 202 Accepted with a job id, and let a worker process it.

Example: An admin clicks "recalculate all scores". The API creates a job and returns at once; a worker processes the records in batches and the UI polls /jobs/:id for progress.

Common mistake: Wrapping the loop in an async function or Promise and thinking it no longer blocks. It still runs on the main thread.

Interview tip: Pick the solution by duration: chunks for seconds, a worker for CPU work, a queue for minutes. That shows judgement.

questions.question: How do you call an API for 1,000 users but only 5 at a time?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use a small pool of workers that each take the next item until the list is empty, or a library such as p-limit.

How it works: Promise.all(users.map(callApi)) starts all 1,000 requests at once. That can trip the other service's rate limit, run out of sockets or memory, and make every request slow. A pool keeps exactly 5 promises in flight: as soon as one finishes, the next starts, and results keep their original order.

Example: Sending a newsletter through an email API that allows 5 concurrent requests: mapLimit(users, 5, sendEmail).

Common mistake: Splitting into batches of 5 with Promise.all per batch. It works, but each batch waits for its slowest call, so it is slower than a real pool.

Interview tip: Mention backpressure on the other service and rate limits; it shows you think about the systems around your code.

questions.question: How do you measure event loop health in production?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Track event loop delay (how late callbacks run) and event loop utilization (how busy the thread is), and alert when they stay high.

How it works: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() gives a histogram of delays; watch p99, not the average. performance.eventLoopUtilization() gives the share of time the loop was busy. Send both to your monitoring (Prometheus, Datadog). To find the cause, take a CPU profile (--cpu-prof) or use Clinic.js Doctor and Flame.

Example: After a release, p99 loop delay jumps from 5 ms to 400 ms; a CPU profile shows a new JSON.stringify of a large object in a logging call.

Common mistake: Only watching CPU percentage. A process can show 25% CPU on a 4-core machine while its single JavaScript thread is 100% busy.

Interview tip: Saying "event loop lag" and "p99" in the same sentence signals production experience.

questions.question: In which event loop phase do setImmediate callbacks run?
questions.answer:
Why C: The check phase exists for setImmediate and comes right after poll.

Why not A: timers is for setTimeout and setInterval.

Why not B: poll runs I/O callbacks such as file reads and incoming data.

Why not D: close callbacks handles events like socket.on('close').

questions.question: Which of these lets I/O and other requests run between chunks of a long job?
questions.answer:
Why D: setImmediate waits for the next turn of the loop, so pending I/O and requests get a chance first.

Why not A, B and C: nextTick and microtasks run before the loop continues, so they never let I/O in between chunks.

questions.question: What is the first argument of a Node.js error-first callback?
options: The error, or null if there was none
questions.correctAnswer: The error, or null if there was none
questions.answer:
Why B: Node passes the error first so you must check it before using the result.

Why not A: The result comes second, after the error.

Why not C: Callbacks for fs, dns and similar APIs have nothing to do with HTTP requests.

Why not D: done() belongs to some libraries (like test frameworks), not to the Node convention.

Fix: if (err) return handle(err);

questions.question: A route runs for (let i = 0; i < 1e9; i++) {}. Why does /health also become slow?
options: The loop blocks the single main thread, so /health waits
Express runs routes one at a time by design
The OS limits Node to one request
questions.correctAnswer: The loop blocks the single main thread, so /health waits
questions.answer:
Why B: All JavaScript callbacks share one thread. Until the loop finishes, no other handler, including /health, can start.

Why not A: The loop does not touch the database at all.

Why not C: Express runs many requests at once as long as none of them blocks the thread.

Why not D: The OS happily accepts many connections; Node just cannot run their handlers.

questions.question: In what order are the logs printed inside this fs.readFile callback?
questions.answer:
Why B: nextTick runs right after the current callback. The callback ran in poll, and check (setImmediate) comes next; timers wait for the next turn.

Why not A and D: nextTick always runs before any timer or immediate callback.

Why not C: That order can happen in the main module, but inside an I/O callback setImmediate always comes before setTimeout.

questions.question: Inside an I/O callback, which runs first: process.nextTick or a resolved promise's then?
questions.answer:
Why B: Node empties the nextTick queue before the promise microtask queue.

Why not A: Promise callbacks run right after the nextTick queue is empty.

Why not C: setImmediate waits for the check phase, after both queues.

Why not D: The order between the two queues is fixed and documented.

questions.question: How do you export and import code in CommonJS and in ES modules?
questions.answer:
Short answer: CommonJS uses require() and module.exports. ES modules use import and export, the JavaScript standard.

How it works: Node decides the module type per file: .mjs is always ESM, .cjs is always CommonJS, and .js follows "type" in the nearest package.json ("module" means ESM, otherwise CommonJS). CommonJS loads synchronously at run time; ESM imports are static and resolved before the code runs.

Example: An older Express API uses require everywhere. A new project sets "type": "module" and writes import express from 'express'.

Common mistake: Mixing both in one file (require and import together), or forgetting the file extension in ESM relative imports ('./utils.js', not './utils').

Interview tip: Mention that new projects should prefer ESM, but you must be able to read CommonJS because so much existing code uses it.

questions.question: What is the difference between dependencies, devDependencies and peerDependencies?
questions.answer:
Short answer: dependencies are needed to run the app, devDependencies only to build and test it, and peerDependencies are packages a library expects the host app to install.

How it works:
dependencies: express, mongoose, bcryptjs
devDependencies: jest, nodemon, eslint, TypeScript
peerDependencies: react for a React component library
Production installs can skip dev packages with npm install --omit=dev (or npm ci --omit=dev), which makes images smaller and faster to build.

Example: npm install -D nodemon puts nodemon in devDependencies; the server on Render does not need it to run.

Common mistake: Putting a runtime package such as dotenv or mongoose in devDependencies; it works locally and crashes in production with "Cannot find module".

Interview tip: Explain peerDependencies with a concrete case; it is the part most candidates cannot explain.
questions.codeSnippet:
npm install express          # dependencies
npm install -D jest nodemon  # devDependencies

questions.question: What do the ^ and ~ symbols mean in package.json versions?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Versions follow semver (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). ^ allows minor and patch updates, ~ allows only patch updates.

How it works:
^1.4.2: any 1.x.x from 1.4.2 up, never 2.0.0
~1.4.2: any 1.4.x from 1.4.2 up
1.4.2: exactly that version
A major version change means breaking changes, so ^ never crosses it. For 0.x packages, ^0.4.2 only allows 0.4.x, because in 0.x every minor change may break things.

Example: "express": "^5.1.0" can install 5.2.0 on a fresh install, but your package-lock.json keeps everyone on the exact version you tested.

Common mistake: Thinking ^ protects you from all breaking changes. Packages sometimes break things in a minor release; the lock file and tests are the real protection.

Interview tip: Mention the 0.x rule; it is a small detail that shows you have read semver properly.

questions.question: Why should you commit package-lock.json, and what is npm ci?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The lock file records the exact version of every package in the tree, so everyone installs identical code. npm ci installs exactly what the lock file says.

How it works: package.json has ranges (^5.1.0); without a lock file two installs a week apart can get different versions. npm ci deletes node_modules, installs exactly from the lock file, fails if package.json and the lock file disagree, never changes the lock file, and is faster. Use npm install while developing and npm ci in CI and deployment.

Example: A deploy breaks on Friday even though no code changed: a sub-dependency released a buggy patch and the server ran npm install without a lock file.

Common mistake: Adding package-lock.json to .gitignore, or deleting it to "fix" install errors.

Interview tip: Saying "reproducible builds" is the key phrase.
questions.codeSnippet:
# CI / deployment
npm ci --omit=dev

questions.question: How does require() find a module?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Core modules first, then relative or absolute file paths, then node_modules folders walking up the directory tree.

How it works: 1) Core modules such as fs or node:http are returned directly.
2) Paths starting with ./, ../ or / load that file, trying .js, .json and .node, or a folder with index.js.
3) Bare names (express) are searched in ./node_modules, then ../node_modules, and so on up to the root.
4) Inside a package, Node uses the "exports" field of its package.json, falling back to "main".

Example: require('./utils/math') loads utils/math.js; require('express') finds node_modules/express and loads the file named in its package.json.

Common mistake: Requiring a file inside a package that its "exports" field does not allow (express/lib/router), which throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED.

Interview tip: Mention require.resolve('name') to see which file Node would load; it is the quickest way to debug a wrong module.
questions.codeSnippet:
require('node:fs');      // core
require('./utils/math'); // ./utils/math.js
require('express');      // node_modules/express via package.json
require.resolve('express'); // the path Node will load

questions.question: What is module caching in Node.js, and how is it useful?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The first require() of a file runs it and caches its module.exports; every later require() returns the same object without running the code again.

How it works: The cache is keyed by the resolved file path. This makes modules natural singletons: a db.js that connects to MongoDB connects once, and a config.js is read once. ES modules are cached the same way.

Example: A logger module creates one pino instance; every file that requires it shares the same logger and settings.

Common mistake: Expecting a module's top-level code to run again for each require, or changing a shared exported object in one file and being surprised that another file sees the change.

Interview tip: Connect this to the singleton pattern; interviewers often ask how you share one DB connection across files.

questions.question: What is the difference between module.exports and exports?
questions.answer:
Short answer: exports is only a shortcut variable that points to module.exports at the start. require() always returns module.exports.

How it works: Adding properties through exports (exports.add = ...) changes the same object, so it works. Assigning a new value to exports (exports = {...}) only changes the local variable; module.exports still points to the original empty object, and the new value is lost.

Example: A file ends with exports = { sub }; another file requires it and gets {}. Calling sub() then throws "sub is not a function".

Common mistake: Mixing both styles in one file, or assigning to exports when exporting a single function or class.

Interview tip: Explain the module wrapper: function (exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname). Then the behaviour is obvious.
questions.codeSnippet:
exports.add = (a, b) => a + b;     // works
exports = { sub: (a, b) => a - b }; // lost: require() never sees it
module.exports = { sub };          // works

questions.question: What happens with circular dependencies in CommonJS, and how do you fix them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: When two modules require each other, the second require returns the first module's exports as they are at that moment: unfinished, often empty.

How it works: a.js starts, requires b.js; b.js requires a.js, but a is still loading, so b gets a's partial module.exports. If b calls a function from a during loading, it is undefined. If it only calls it later, it may work, which makes the bug confusing.

Example: user.model.js requires order.model.js to validate orders, and order.model.js requires user.model.js: one of them sees {} and crashes with "x is not a function" on startup.

Common mistake: "Fixing" it by moving require calls around until it happens to work, instead of removing the cycle.

Interview tip: Fixes to name: move shared code into a third module, require inside the function that needs it, or redesign so dependencies point one way. Tools like madge can find cycles.

questions.question: How do you use ES modules in Node and mix them with CommonJS?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Set "type": "module" in package.json or use .mjs files. ESM can import CommonJS easily; CommonJS loads ESM with await import(), or with require() in newer Node versions.

How it works:
Importing CommonJS from ESM: module.exports becomes the default export, and Node tries to detect named exports.
Loading ESM from CommonJS: await import('./x.mjs') always works; Node 22.12+ (and 20.19+) can also require() ES modules that do not use top-level await.
In ESM, relative imports need the file extension, and __dirname, require and module are not available.

Example: An ESM app imports an old CommonJS helper library with import pkg from 'old-lib' and then reads pkg.someFunction.

Common mistake: Writing import './utils' without .js in ESM, which fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.

Interview tip: Mention top-level await as a reason ESM cannot always be required synchronously.

questions.question: How do you keep npm dependencies secure?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Lock versions, install with npm ci, scan with npm audit, keep dependencies few and updated, and be careful with install scripts.

How it works:
Lock file + npm ci: everyone runs the same, reviewed versions
npm audit: lists known vulnerabilities; fix critical ones first
Dependabot or Renovate: small, regular update pull requests
Before adding a package: check downloads, maintainers, last release and size
Install scripts: npm ci --ignore-scripts in CI where possible, since malicious packages often run code on install
Tokens: never commit .npmrc with an auth token

Example: A popular package's maintainer account is hacked and a new version steals environment variables during install. Teams that pinned versions and reviewed updates were not affected.

Common mistake: Running npm audit fix --force blindly; it can jump major versions and break the app.

Interview tip: Mention supply-chain attacks by name; it shows you know the real risk, not only CVEs.
questions.codeSnippet:
npm audit --omit=dev
npm audit fix
npm ci --ignore-scripts

questions.question: Which command installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json, which suits CI?
questions.answer:
Why C: npm ci installs exactly from the lock file and fails if it does not match package.json.

Why not A: npm install may update the lock file when ranges allow newer versions.

Why not B: npm update deliberately moves packages to newer versions.

Why not D: npm audit only reports vulnerabilities; it installs nothing.

questions.question: Which version can "^1.4.2" install?
questions.answer:
Why B: ^ allows newer minor and patch versions within the same major: 1.4.2 up to, but not including, 2.0.0.

Why not A: 2.0.0 is a new major version, which may contain breaking changes.

Why not C and D: Versions below 1.4.2 are never chosen.

questions.question: Where should jest and nodemon be listed in package.json?
questions.answer:
Why B: They are only needed while developing and testing, so production installs can skip them.

Why not A: dependencies are installed in production too, making the deploy bigger for nothing.

Why not C: peerDependencies are for libraries asking the host app to provide a package.

Why not D: scripts holds commands such as "test": "jest", not packages.

questions.question: What does main.js print?
questions.answer:
Why B: count was copied into the exported object when counter.js loaded. inc() changes the module's local variable, not that copy.

Why not A: That would need a live binding (ES modules) or a getter.

Why not C: count was set to 0 in the exported object, so it is defined.

Why not D: Nothing here calls an undefined function.

questions.question: What does require() return for a module that only contains exports = { a: 1 }?
questions.answer:
Why B: Assigning to exports only changes the local variable. require() returns module.exports, which is still the original empty object.

Why not A: That would need module.exports = { a: 1 }.

Why not C: module.exports always starts as an empty object, never undefined.

Why not D: The code is valid JavaScript; it just does not export anything.

questions.question: Three files require the same module. How many times does its top-level code run?
options: Never, until a function is called
questions.answer:
Why B: The first require runs the module and caches its exports; the other two get the cached object.

Why not A: That would happen only if the cache were cleared between requires.

Why not C: Top-level code runs as soon as the module is first required.

Why not D: Modules are loaded at require time, not per HTTP request.

questions.question: What is EventEmitter in Node.js?
questions.answer:
Short answer: EventEmitter is the class behind Node's event system: on() adds a listener, emit() calls the listeners of an event, once() listens one time and off() removes a listener.

How it works: Many core objects extend it: HTTP servers ('request'), streams ('data', 'end'), sockets and process ('SIGTERM'). Listeners run synchronously, in the order they were added, when emit() is called. You can extend it in your own classes to let other parts of the app react to what happens.

Example: After a user registers, the auth service emits 'userRegistered'; separate listeners send a welcome email and record analytics, so the register code does not need to know about them.

Common mistake: Assuming emit() is async. Listeners run immediately inside emit(), so a slow listener slows down the code that emitted.

Interview tip: Mention that this is the observer pattern; then give the decoupling example.

questions.question: What happens when an EventEmitter emits 'error' and nobody is listening?
questions.answer:
Short answer: 'error' is special: with no listener, Node throws the error, and if nothing catches it the process crashes.

How it works: Other events with no listeners are simply ignored. For 'error', Node assumes an unhandled error is dangerous and throws it. Streams, sockets and servers all emit 'error', so each one you create should have an 'error' listener (or be used with stream.pipeline, which handles it).

Example: A route streams a file with fs.createReadStream(path).pipe(res). A user requests a file that does not exist, the stream emits ENOENT, and the whole server crashes for every user.

Common mistake: Wrapping createReadStream in try/catch. The error happens later, asynchronously, so the try/catch never sees it.

Interview tip: Mention events.once and events.on helpers; they turn 'error' into a rejected promise, which is easier to handle with await.

questions.question: What is a Buffer, and why does Node need it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A Buffer is a fixed-size block of raw bytes. Node needs it because files, network data and images are bytes, not JavaScript strings.

How it works: Buffers live outside the normal V8 heap and are a subclass of Uint8Array. You convert between bytes and text with an encoding: Buffer.from('hi', 'utf8'), buf.toString('base64'). length is in bytes, not characters, so non-English text takes more bytes than letters.

Example: Sending an image as base64 in JSON: Buffer.from(fileBytes).toString('base64'). Comparing a webhook signature with crypto.timingSafeEqual takes two Buffers.

Common mistake: Using string length to check a size limit, or creating a buffer with the old new Buffer(size) API, which is deprecated and could expose old memory.

Interview tip: Mention that Buffer.alloc(size) is zero-filled (safe) and Buffer.allocUnsafe(size) is faster but may contain old data.
questions.codeSnippet:
const buf = Buffer.from('Salam');
buf.length;                 // 5 bytes
buf.toString('base64');     // 'U2FsYW0='
Buffer.from('é').length;    // 2 (UTF-8 uses 2 bytes)

questions.question: What are the four types of streams? Give a real example of each.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Readable, Writable, Duplex and Transform.

How it works:
Readable: data comes out; fs.createReadStream, an incoming HTTP request (req)
Writable: data goes in; fs.createWriteStream, an HTTP response (res)
Duplex: reads and writes independently; a TCP socket
Transform: a Duplex that changes data on the way through; zlib.createGzip, a CSV parser

Example: Download log: fs.createReadStream (Readable) -> zlib.createGzip (Transform) -> res (Writable), so a 1 GB log is compressed and sent without loading it into memory.

Common mistake: Mixing up Duplex and Transform. In a Duplex the two sides are unrelated (a socket); in a Transform the output is calculated from the input.

Interview tip: Always give one real example per type; definitions alone sound memorised.
questions.codeSnippet:
fs.createReadStream('big.log')   // Readable
  .pipe(zlib.createGzip())        // Transform
  .pipe(fs.createWriteStream('big.log.gz')); // Writable

questions.question: Why should you use streams instead of fs.readFile for large files?
questions.answer:
Short answer: fs.readFile loads the whole file into memory before you can use it; a stream handles it in small chunks, so memory stays low and data starts flowing at once.

How it works: A Readable file stream reads 64 KB at a time by default and passes each chunk on. Memory use stays about the same whether the file is 1 MB or 10 GB, and the user starts receiving data immediately instead of after the whole file is read.

Example: Ten users download a 500 MB video. With readFile the server needs about 5 GB of RAM and crashes; with streams it needs a few MB.

Common mistake: Reading a stream into one big string with data events (body += chunk), which brings back the same memory problem.

Interview tip: Quote the numbers (chunk size, memory per user); it makes the answer concrete.

questions.question: What does the warning "MaxListenersExceededWarning" usually mean?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Node warns when more than 10 listeners are added to one event on one emitter. It usually points to a memory leak.

How it works: The limit exists to catch code that adds a listener again and again without removing it, for example inside a request handler. Each listener keeps its closure (and everything it references) alive. setMaxListeners can raise the limit when many listeners are truly expected, but it should not be used to hide the warning.

Example: A middleware adds process.on('SIGTERM', ...) on every request. After 11 requests the warning appears; after a day, memory has grown by thousands of closures.

Common mistake: Raising the limit to 100 to make the warning go away.

Interview tip: Say how you would find it: run with --trace-warnings to see the stack that added the listener.

questions.question: What is backpressure, and how does Node deal with it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Backpressure is when data comes in faster than it can be written out. Node signals it with write() returning false, and you must pause until the 'drain' event.

How it works: Every writable stream has an internal buffer (highWaterMark, 16 KB by default for byte streams). write() adds data and returns false once the buffer is full. If you keep writing anyway, data piles up in memory. pipe(), stream.pipeline() and for await...of handle this for you by pausing the source and resuming on 'drain'.

Example: A server reads a 1 GB video from a fast SSD and sends it to a user on slow mobile data. Without backpressure the whole file sits in RAM; with 100 such users the server crashes.

Common mistake: Writing in a 'data' handler and ignoring the return value of write().

Interview tip: Mention that pipeline and async iteration handle backpressure automatically, which is why they are the recommended way.

questions.question: Why is stream.pipeline better than .pipe()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: pipeline forwards errors from any stream, destroys every stream in the chain on failure and tells you when everything is finished. .pipe() does none of that.

How it works: With .pipe(), an error in a middle stream does not reach the others: the source may keep a file handle open and the response may hang forever. You would need an 'error' listener on every stream. pipeline() from node:stream/promises returns a promise that rejects on the first error and resolves when the last stream finishes.

Example: A gzip download route uses .pipe(). The client disconnects halfway; with .pipe() the file stream stays open and leaks a file descriptor each time. With pipeline everything is cleaned up.

Common mistake: Using .pipe() and adding an 'error' handler only on the last stream.

Interview tip: Say "pipeline is .pipe() plus error handling and cleanup"; it is a clear one-liner.

questions.question: A user uploads a 2 GB CSV file. How would you process it in Node?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Never load it into memory: stream the upload to storage, then stream the file through a CSV parser and insert rows in batches, ideally as a background job.

How it works:
Upload: stream to disk or S3 (busboy, multer disk storage, or a pre-signed S3 URL so the file never touches the API)
Parse: read the stored file as a stream with csv-parse
Insert: collect about 1,000 rows and insertMany; awaiting each batch pauses reading (backpressure)
Respond: return 202 Accepted with a job id; a worker processes it and the UI polls for progress
Validate: count and report bad rows instead of failing the whole file

Example: An admin imports a product catalogue of 3 million rows; memory stays around 100 MB and the API stays responsive.

Common mistake: Using multer's default memory storage, which puts the whole 2 GB file in RAM.

Interview tip: Interviewers want to hear four words: stream, batch, backpressure, background job.

questions.question: How do you write your own Transform stream?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create a Transform and implement transform(chunk, encoding, callback): change the chunk and pass the result to the callback.

How it works: callback(null, result) sends one output chunk; you can also call this.push() several times and then callback(). Passing an error to the callback fails the stream (and the pipeline). An optional flush(callback) runs at the end to output any leftover data. objectMode: true lets the stream pass JavaScript objects instead of bytes.

Example: A log-export route uses a Transform that masks email addresses before the data reaches the user, without loading the logs into memory.

Common mistake: Forgetting that a chunk can end in the middle of a line or a multi-byte character; real parsers keep the leftover part and handle it in the next chunk or in flush().

Interview tip: Mention objectMode and flush; they show you have built one, not only read about it.

questions.question: Which EventEmitter method adds a listener that runs only one time?
questions.answer:
Why B: once() removes the listener automatically after its first call.

Why not A: on() keeps the listener until you remove it.

Why not C: emit() triggers an event; it does not add a listener.

Why not D: There is no addOnce method in Node's EventEmitter.

questions.question: Which stream type reads and writes and changes the data passing through?
questions.answer:
Why D: A Transform computes its output from its input, like gzip or a CSV parser.

Why not A: A Readable only produces data.

Why not B: A Writable only consumes data.

Why not C: A Duplex reads and writes, but the two sides are unrelated, like a socket.

questions.question: What happens when 'error' is emitted on an emitter with no 'error' listener?
options: It is logged as a warning
The error is thrown and can crash the process
questions.correctAnswer: The error is thrown and can crash the process
questions.answer:
Why C: Node treats 'error' specially: without a listener, it throws, and an uncaught throw crashes the process.

Why not A: Other events are ignored without listeners, but 'error' is not.

Why not B: There is no warning; it is a real throw.

Why not D: Emitters never retry anything by themselves.

Fix: Add stream.on('error', handler), or use stream.pipeline.

questions.question: What does Buffer.from('é').length return?
questions.answer:
Why B: Buffer length counts bytes, and 'é' takes 2 bytes in UTF-8.

Why not A: 1 is the string length ('é'.length), not the byte length.

Why not C: 4 bytes are used only by characters such as many emoji.

Why not D: Every Buffer has a numeric length.

questions.question: writable.write() returned false. What should your code do?
options: Stop writing and wait for the drain event
questions.correctAnswer: Stop writing and wait for the drain event
questions.answer:
Why B: false means the internal buffer is full. Pause the source and continue when 'drain' fires.

Why not A: Writing more makes memory grow; that is the problem backpressure prevents.

Why not C: The stream is fine; it only needs time to flush.

Why not D: The data was accepted, but false is a request to slow down.

Fix: Use stream.pipeline or for await...of, which do this for you.

questions.question: Why prefer stream.pipeline() over .pipe()?
options: It passes errors on and destroys all streams on failure
questions.correctAnswer: It passes errors on and destroys all streams on failure
questions.answer:
Why B: pipeline adds error forwarding, cleanup of every stream and a completion callback or promise.

Why not A: Speed is the same; the difference is safety.

Why not C: It works with any streams: HTTP, sockets, zlib, files.

Why not D: It keeps backpressure, exactly like .pipe().

questions.question: What is Express, and why use it instead of the plain http module?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express is a small web framework on top of Node's http module that adds routing, middleware and helpers for requests and responses.

How it works: With plain http you parse the URL, method, query string, JSON body and headers yourself, and write one big if/else for routes. Express gives you app.get('/users/:id'), req.params, req.query, res.json(), res.status() and a middleware chain for shared logic such as auth and logging.

Example: A 30-route API in plain http becomes hard to read; in Express each route is one line plus a controller function, grouped with Routers.

Common mistake: Thinking Express replaces Node. It is a thin layer; req and res are still Node's objects with extra methods.

Interview tip: Mention alternatives (Fastify for speed, NestJS for structure) and why you would still pick Express: simple and huge ecosystem.

questions.question: What is middleware in Express?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Middleware is a function (req, res, next) that runs during a request and either sends a response or calls next() to continue.

How it works: Express keeps a list of middleware and route handlers. Each one can read or change req and res (for example set req.user), end the request (res.json), or call next() to pass control on. next(err) skips to the error handler. Body parsing, CORS, authentication, logging and rate limiting are all middleware.

Example: A request logger records method, path, status and duration for every request without touching any route.

Common mistake: Forgetting to call next() (the request hangs) or calling it after sending a response ("headers already sent").

Interview tip: Describe it as a pipeline: request -> middleware 1 -> middleware 2 -> route -> response.

questions.question: Why does the order of middleware matter in Express? Give real bugs it causes.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express runs middleware in the exact order you register it, so the wrong order silently breaks features.

How it works: Real bugs:
Body parser after routes: req.body is undefined in every handler
Auth after the route: the route is public by accident
404 handler before routes: every request returns 404
Error handler not last: errors are never caught by it
CORS after auth: preflight OPTIONS requests fail with 401

Example: A team adds app.use(protect) at the bottom of app.js "for all routes"; nothing is protected because every route above it already responded.

Common mistake: Assuming app.use order does not matter because "Express figures it out".

Interview tip: Recite the safe order: security headers, CORS, body parser, logging, rate limit, routes, 404, error handler.
questions.codeSnippet:
app.use(express.json());           // 1. parse body
app.use('/api', authRoutes);       // 2. routes
app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ message: 'Not found' })); // 3. 404
app.use(errorHandler);             // 4. errors, always last

questions.question: What is the difference between req.params, req.query and req.body?
questions.answer:
Short answer: req.params holds named parts of the path, req.query holds the query string, and req.body holds the parsed request body.

How it works: /users/:id gives req.params.id
?page=2&sort=name gives req.query.page and req.query.sort
A JSON body gives req.body, but only after a body parser such as express.json() runs
Params and query values are always strings (or arrays), so convert numbers yourself.

Example: PUT /users/42?notify=true with body { "name": "Sara" }: params.id is '42', query.notify is 'true' (a string, not a boolean), body.name is 'Sara'.

Common mistake: Comparing req.query.notify === true, which is never true because it is the string 'true'. Another: trusting these values without validation.

Interview tip: Mention that all three come from the user and must be validated; that is the follow-up interviewers want.

questions.question: How does error-handling middleware work in Express?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It is middleware with four arguments (err, req, res, next). Express jumps to it when you call next(err) or when a handler throws.

How it works: Express recognises it by the four arguments, so keep next in the signature even if unused. Register it after all routes. In Express 5, rejected promises from async handlers also reach it automatically. A good handler sets the status code, logs unexpected errors with the stack, and sends a safe JSON message.

Example: A controller throws new AppError('Email already registered', 409); the error handler returns { message } with 409, while a database crash returns 500 with "Something went wrong" and the details go only to the logs.

Common mistake: Sending err.stack or raw database errors to the client in production; it leaks file paths and internals to attackers.

Interview tip: Mention one central handler instead of try/catch with res.status(500) in every route.

questions.question: What is express.Router, and why use it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Router is a mini app with its own routes and middleware that you mount under a path prefix.

How it works: It lets you split a large API into files by feature (auth, users, admin) and apply middleware to a whole group at once with router.use(). Routers can be nested, and a router mounted at /api/admin only sees requests under that prefix.

Example: All admin routes need login and the admin role: router.use(protect, adminOnly) at the top of routes/admin.js protects every route in that file with one line.

Common mistake: Adding protect to each admin route by hand and forgetting one, which leaves it open.

Interview tip: Mention mergeParams: true when a nested router needs params from its parent (/users/:userId/orders).

questions.question: What causes "Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client"?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The code tried to send a second response for the same request.

How it works: Once res.json(), res.send() or res.end() runs, the headers are on their way to the client; any later attempt to set a status or send again throws this error. Usual causes: no return after a response inside an if, calling next() after responding, or both a callback and a promise responding.

Example: A route returns 404 when the user is missing but forgets return, so it continues to res.json(user) and crashes the request with this error.

Common mistake: Silencing it with if (!res.headersSent) everywhere instead of fixing the flow.

Interview tip: Show the fix pattern: return res.status(...).json(...), so every response is also an exit.

questions.question: Write an Express middleware that checks a JWT and gives routes the logged-in user.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read the Bearer token, verify it, load the user, check they may still log in, attach them to req.user and call next(); respond 401 otherwise.

How it works: Steps: read Authorization: Bearer <token>; jwt.verify with the secret (throws if changed or expired); load the user from the database so a deleted or blocked account is refused even with a valid token; set req.user; call next(). Any failure returns 401 with a clear message.

Example: This project's protect middleware also rejects tokens issued before the last password reset, so changing the password logs out stolen sessions.

Common mistake: Only decoding the token with jwt.decode() (no signature check), or trusting the role inside the token without loading the user.

Interview tip: Mention the extra checks (blocked user, password changed); they separate a production answer from a tutorial answer.

questions.question: How do you make a reusable middleware that takes options, such as a role check?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Write a function that takes the options and returns the real (req, res, next) middleware; the options stay available through a closure.

How it works: This is the middleware factory pattern. express.json({ limit }), cors({ origin }) and rateLimit({ windowMs }) all work this way. It keeps one tested implementation and lets each route configure it.

Example: requireRole('admin') on delete routes and requireRole('admin', 'editor') on content routes, both from the same function.

Common mistake: Writing a separate adminOnly, editorOnly and managerOnly middleware with copied code.

Interview tip: Name the pattern (factory + closure); interviewers often follow up with "how does it remember the roles?"

questions.question: What changed in Express 5 that matters for interviews and upgrades?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Async errors are handled automatically, route path syntax is stricter, and old deprecated APIs were removed.

How it works:
Async errors: a rejected promise or throw in an async handler goes to the error middleware, so asyncHandler wrappers are no longer needed
Paths: wildcards need a name (/*splat), and ? + ( ) are no longer special pattern characters in strings
req.body: undefined (not {}) when no body parser ran
Removed: res.send(status), app.del, res.sendfile and similar old APIs
Node: requires Node 18 or newer

Example: Upgrading an API from Express 4 to 5: remove asyncHandler, rename app.get('*') to app.get('/*splat'), and fix any code that assumed req.body is always an object.

Common mistake: Upgrading the version number and not testing wildcard routes; they fail at startup with a path-to-regexp error.

Interview tip: Lead with async error handling; it is the change that most affects daily code.

questions.question: Which built-in middleware parses JSON request bodies?
questions.answer:
Why B: express.json() reads JSON bodies and puts the result in req.body.

Why not A: express.static() serves files from a folder.

Why not C: express.urlencoded() parses HTML form bodies (a=1&b=2), not JSON.

Why not D: express.Router() creates a group of routes.

questions.question: For GET /users/7?tab=posts with the route /users/:id, where is the value "posts"?
questions.answer:
Why C: Everything after ? is the query string, which Express puts in req.query.

Why not A: req.params only has the named path parts, here id = '7'.

Why not B: GET requests normally have no body.

Why not D: Headers are separate from the URL.

questions.question: How many arguments does an Express error-handling middleware take?
questions.answer:
Why C: (err, req, res, next). Express recognises an error handler by its four arguments.

Why not A and B: A normal middleware has three (req, res, next); with fewer than four Express treats it as normal middleware and skips it for errors.

Why not D: There is no five-argument form.

Fix: Keep next in the signature even if you never call it.

questions.question: What happens if a middleware neither sends a response nor calls next()?
options: The request hangs until it times out
questions.correctAnswer: The request hangs until it times out
questions.answer:
Why B: The chain simply stops. The client waits for a response that never comes, until a timeout.

Why not A: Express never calls next() on your behalf.

Why not C: The 404 handler would only run if next() reached it.

Why not D: Nothing throws, so nothing crashes; it just hangs.

questions.question: The error "Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client" usually means what?
options: A response was sent twice for one request
questions.correctAnswer: A response was sent twice for one request
questions.answer:
Why B: The code reached a second res.json(), res.send() or res.status() after a response was already sent.

Why not A: Invalid JSON gives a parse error, not this one.

Why not C: CORS problems show in the browser, not as this server error.

Why not D: A closed connection gives errors like ECONNRESET or 'aborted'.

Fix: Use return res.status(...).json(...) in every branch.

questions.question: In Express 5, an async route handler throws an error. What happens?
options: The error goes to the error-handling middleware automatically
Express sends 200 with an empty body
questions.correctAnswer: The error goes to the error-handling middleware automatically
questions.answer:
Why C: Express 5 watches the promise returned by handlers and forwards rejections to the error middleware.

Why not A: That was Express 4's behaviour without a wrapper.

Why not B: The rejection is handled by Express, so it is not an unhandled rejection.

Why not D: Express never turns an error into a success response.

questions.question: What is a REST API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A REST API exposes resources (users, orders) at URLs and uses HTTP methods as the actions, with stateless requests and standard status codes.

How it works: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes. Stateless means each request carries everything the server needs, such as the auth token, so any server instance can handle it. Responses use status codes and usually JSON.

Example: An e-commerce API: GET /api/orders lists, POST /api/orders creates, PATCH /api/orders/42 changes the status, DELETE /api/orders/42 cancels.

Common mistake: Designing every endpoint as POST /doSomething (RPC style) and still calling it REST.

Interview tip: Mention statelessness and why it helps scaling (any server can answer any request).
questions.codeSnippet:
GET    /api/orders        list orders
POST   /api/orders        create an order
GET    /api/orders/42     one order
PATCH  /api/orders/42     change some fields
DELETE /api/orders/42     delete it

questions.question: Which HTTP status codes should an API use, and when?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use the code that matches what happened: 2xx success, 4xx the client's mistake, 5xx the server's mistake.

How it works: The ones you need:
200 OK: a read or update worked
201 Created: POST created something (send the new item back)
204 No Content: success with nothing to return (DELETE)
400 Bad Request: invalid input
401 Unauthorized: not logged in or token expired
403 Forbidden: logged in but not allowed
404 Not Found: the item does not exist
409 Conflict: duplicate, e.g. email already registered
422 Unprocessable: valid JSON but it breaks a rule
429 Too Many Requests: rate limit hit
500 Internal Server Error: a bug or crash on the server

Example: A signup API returns 201 with the new user, 400 if the email is missing, 409 if it is already registered and 429 after too many attempts.

Common mistake: Returning 200 with { error: "..." }. Frontend code, monitoring and retries all trust the status code, so the failure looks like a success.

Interview tip: Explain 401 vs 403 before you are asked; it is the most common follow-up.

questions.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
questions.answer:
Short answer: PUT replaces the whole resource with what you send; PATCH changes only the fields you send.

How it works: With PUT, fields you leave out are removed or reset, so the client must send the full object. With PATCH, missing fields stay as they are. Both should be idempotent in a good design: sending the same request twice gives the same result.

Example: Profile { name: 'Ali', city: 'Lahore' }. PATCH { city: 'Karachi' } keeps the name. PUT { city: 'Karachi' } leaves an object without a name.

Common mistake: Implementing PUT like PATCH (or the other way round), so clients get surprised when data disappears.

Interview tip: Say which one you use for "edit profile" (PATCH) and why.

questions.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
questions.answer:
Short answer: 401 means "we do not know who you are" (not authenticated). 403 means "we know who you are, and you are not allowed" (not authorised).

How it works: 401 Unauthorized is badly named: it is about authentication. No token, an expired token or a bad token gives 401, and logging in may fix it. 403 Forbidden is about permissions: the user is logged in, but their role or ownership does not allow the action, so logging in again will not help.

Example: A normal user calls DELETE /api/admin/users/5 with a valid token: 403. A visitor calls it without a token: 401.

Common mistake: Returning 401 for permission problems; the frontend then logs the user out instead of showing "not allowed".

Interview tip: Some APIs return 404 instead of 403 for other users' private items so they do not reveal that the item exists; mention it as a bonus.
questions.codeSnippet:
if (!req.user) return res.status(401).json({ message: 'Please log in' });
if (req.user.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).json({ message: 'Admins only' });

questions.question: How should you design REST URLs?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use plural nouns for resources, let the HTTP method be the verb, and put filters, sorting and paging in the query string.

How it works:
Nouns, not verbs: /orders, not /getOrders
Plural: /users/42
Nesting only for clear ownership: /users/42/orders
Query for options: /orders?status=paid&sort=-createdAt&page=2
Actions that are not CRUD: a sub-resource such as POST /orders/42/cancel
Lowercase with hyphens: /order-items

Example: Instead of GET /getPaidOrdersForUser?id=42, use GET /users/42/orders?status=paid.

Common mistake: Nesting too deep (/users/1/orders/2/items/3/reviews); keep it to one level and use top-level resources with filters.

Interview tip: Mention consistency: one style across the whole API matters more than any single rule.

questions.question: What is idempotency, and why does it matter?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An operation is idempotent if doing it once or many times leaves the same final state.

How it works: GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent; POST usually is not, because each call creates something new. It matters because networks fail: browsers, mobile apps, load balancers and your own retry code resend requests. A retried PUT is harmless; a retried POST can create two orders or charge a card twice.

Example: A payment request times out on the client but actually succeeded on the server. The app retries, and without protection the customer pays twice.

Common mistake: Retrying POST requests automatically in an HTTP client without an idempotency key.

Interview tip: Connect idempotency to retries and give the payment example; that is what interviewers are checking.
questions.codeSnippet:
PUT /users/1 { "name": "Ali" }  // 5 times -> same result
POST /orders { ... }             // 5 times -> 5 orders!

questions.question: Offset vs cursor pagination: what is the difference, and when does offset fail?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Offset pagination skips N items; cursor pagination asks for items after the last one seen. Offset is simple but slow on deep pages and unstable when data changes.

How it works: Offset (?page=3&limit=20 = skip 40): easy and allows jumping to any page, but the database still walks the skipped rows, and new items shift every page, causing duplicates or gaps. Cursor (?after=<last id>): uses an index to continue exactly where the user stopped, stays fast at any depth and is stable, but cannot jump straight to page 50.

Example: A social feed with infinite scroll uses cursors; an admin table with page numbers uses offsets.

Common mistake: Using skip with large offsets on a big collection, which makes page 10,000 take seconds.

Interview tip: Return the next cursor in the response ({ items, nextCursor }) so the client never builds it itself.

questions.question: How do you version a REST API, and how do you retire an old version?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Put a version in the URL (/api/v1) or in a header, create a new version only for breaking changes, and retire old versions with a published date and warning headers.

How it works: URL versioning is the most common because it is visible and easy to route. Adding fields is not breaking; renaming or removing fields, changing types or changing behaviour is. To retire a version: announce a date, send Deprecation and Sunset headers, log which clients still call it, contact them, then remove it.

Example: A mobile app cannot force every user to update, so v1 stays alive for months while new app versions use v2.

Common mistake: Making breaking changes in place, which breaks old mobile apps that users have not updated.

Interview tip: Mention mobile clients; they are the main reason versioning exists.

questions.question: How do you validate input in an Express API and return useful errors?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Validate body, query and params with a schema in middleware before the controller, keep only known fields, and return 400 with a list of field errors.

How it works: Libraries such as zod, Joi or express-validator describe the expected shape once. The middleware converts types (page '2' to 2), strips unknown fields (so nobody can sneak in role: 'admin'), and returns errors like [{ field: 'email', message: 'Invalid email' }] so the frontend can show each one next to its input.

Example: A register form sends an invalid email and a short password; the API returns both errors at once, and the form highlights both fields.

Common mistake: Validating only on the frontend. Anyone can call the API directly with curl or Postman.

Interview tip: Mention mass assignment as the security reason for stripping unknown fields.

questions.question: A mobile app sends "create order" twice because of a bad network. How do you prevent a duplicate order?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use an idempotency key: the client sends the same unique key with every retry, and the server returns the saved result instead of creating a second order.

How it works: The app creates a UUID per checkout and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key, the user and the response, with a unique index on (key, user). If the key is seen again, it returns the stored response. The unique index also stops two parallel retries from both succeeding.

Example: Stripe and other payment APIs work exactly this way; a retried charge with the same key never charges twice.

Common mistake: Checking for "a similar order in the last minute" instead; it blocks real repeat orders and still fails under race conditions.

Interview tip: Mention the unique index for race conditions; that is the detail most answers miss.

questions.question: What is the difference between REST and gRPC, and when would you use each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: REST exposes resources over plain HTTP, usually with JSON, so any client (including browsers) can call it and people can read it. gRPC calls remote functions defined in a .proto file, sends binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, and generates typed clients; it is faster and supports streaming, but browsers need a gRPC-Web proxy.

How it works:
Contract: REST is often documented with OpenAPI; gRPC has a required .proto file
Format: REST sends JSON text; gRPC sends compact binary messages
Transport: gRPC needs HTTP/2 and supports streaming in both directions
Tooling: REST works with curl and the browser; gRPC needs generated clients or special tools
Typical use: REST for public and browser-facing APIs, gRPC for internal service-to-service calls

Example: A MERN app's React frontend calls the Express REST API. Inside the backend, the order service calls the payment service with gRPC because it is fast and strictly typed.

Common mistake: Saying gRPC "replaces" REST everywhere. For a normal web app with a browser client, REST (or GraphQL) is simpler.

Interview tip: Mention the cost of switching: a .proto contract, code generation and harder debugging, which pays off only with many internal services.

questions.question: Design a scalable REST API for a social media app with millions of users.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Start with clear resources and endpoints, keep the API servers stateless behind a load balancer, add caching and good indexes, use cursor pagination, move slow work to queues, and protect it with rate limits. Then explain how the feed is built, because that is the hardest part.

How it works:
Resources: /users, /posts, /posts/:id/comments, /users/:id/followers, /feed
Stateless servers: JWT auth, no sessions in memory, so you can add servers behind a load balancer
Pagination: cursor based (?after=<lastId>&limit=20), never skip/offset on huge collections
Database: indexes for every main query; shard or partition big collections like posts by user id
Caching: Redis for hot data (profiles, counters), a CDN for images and videos
Feed: fan-out on write (push post ids into followers' feeds) for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities with millions of followers
Async work: a queue for notifications, image resizing and search indexing
Safety: rate limits per user and IP, idempotency keys for POSTs that may be retried

Example: GET /api/feed?after=abc&limit=20 reads 20 post ids from the user's Redis feed list, loads the posts in one query and returns nextCursor for the next page.

Common mistake: Jumping into a database choice before asking about scale and read/write patterns, or using offset pagination that gets slower on every page.

Interview tip: Ask about numbers first (daily users, reads vs writes), state the trade-offs (consistency vs speed for likes and counters), and draw the request flow.

questions.question: Which HTTP method should create a new resource?
questions.answer:
Why B: POST /orders creates a new order, and the server chooses its id.

Why not A: GET only reads and must not change data.

Why not C: PUT replaces a resource at a known URL; it is not the usual way to create with a server-chosen id.

Why not D: DELETE removes a resource.

questions.question: A DELETE succeeds and returns no body. Which status code fits best?
questions.answer:
Why C: 204 No Content means the request worked and there is nothing to send back.

Why not A: 200 is fine if you return a body, but with no body 204 is clearer.

Why not B: 201 is for creating something.

Why not D: 404 means the item was not found.
