questions.question: A logged-in user tries to open an admin-only route. Which status code should you return?
questions.answer:
Why C: The user is known but not allowed: that is 403 Forbidden.

Why not A: 400 is for invalid input.

Why not B: 401 means not logged in; this user is logged in.

Why not D: 404 is sometimes used to hide private items, but for an admin route 403 is the honest answer.

questions.question: Which set of methods should be idempotent?
questions.answer:
Why B: Repeating GET, PUT or DELETE leaves the same final state.

Why not A and C: POST usually creates a new item each time, so it is not idempotent.

Why not D: GET is idempotent, but so are PUT and DELETE.

questions.question: Which pagination stays correct when new items keep being added to the top of a feed?
questions.answer:
Why B: A cursor continues from the last item the user saw, so new items at the top do not shift the next page.

Why not A: New items push everything down, so the next offset page repeats items.

Why not C: Random pages make no sense for a feed.

Why not D: Loading everything does not scale and wastes bandwidth.

questions.question: A client adds "role": "admin" to a profile update request and becomes an admin. What is this bug called?
questions.answer:
Why B: The server copied the whole request body into the user model, including a field the user should never set.

Why not A: CSRF tricks a logged-in browser into sending a request; here the attacker sends it directly.

Why not C: Injection inserts query syntax; here the value is a normal field.

Why not D: Rate limiting is a defence, not a bug.

Fix: Accept only allowed fields (name, city), for example with a validation schema.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Authentication checks who you are; authorization checks what you are allowed to do.

How it works: Authentication happens at login (email + password, Google sign-in) and then on every request through a token or session. Authorization runs after it: roles (admin, user), ownership (you can edit only your own posts) or plans (paid users only). Failing authentication gives 401; failing authorization gives 403.

Example: In this project, protect checks the JWT (authentication), adminOnly checks the role, and per-language access checks whether a user may open a topic (authorization).

Common mistake: Doing authorization only in the frontend by hiding buttons; the API must check it too.

Interview tip: Give one example of role-based and one of ownership-based authorization.
questions.codeSnippet:
router.delete('/users/:id',
  protect,              // authentication: who are you?
  requireRole('admin'), // authorization: may you do this?
  deleteUser);

questions.question: Why do you hash passwords with bcrypt instead of encrypting them or using SHA-256?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Passwords must be stored so that even the server cannot recover them. bcrypt is one-way, salted and deliberately slow, which makes stolen hashes very hard to crack.

How it works: Encryption is reversible: whoever steals the key gets every password. SHA-256 is one-way but very fast, so a GPU can try billions of guesses per second. bcrypt (or argon2) adds a random salt to each password (equal passwords get different hashes) and has a cost factor that makes each guess slow; you can raise it as computers get faster.

Example: A database leak exposes 1 million bcrypt hashes at cost 12. Cracking even weak passwords takes attackers months instead of minutes.

Common mistake: Writing your own scheme with sha256(password + secret), or comparing hashes with === instead of bcrypt.compare.

Interview tip: Mention the cost factor and that a login taking about 100 ms is a deliberate trade-off.
questions.codeSnippet:
const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12); // cost 12, salt included
const ok = await bcrypt.compare(input, hash);

questions.question: How does JWT authentication work?
questions.answer:
Short answer: After login, the server signs a token with the user id and an expiry. The client sends it with every request, and the server verifies the signature instead of looking up a session.

How it works: A JWT has three base64url parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as id and exp) and signature. jwt.verify recomputes the signature with the secret: if anyone changed the payload, or the token has expired, verification fails. The payload is encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it.

Example: Login returns { token }; the React app stores it and sends Authorization: Bearer <token>; the protect middleware verifies it and loads the user.

Common mistake: Putting sensitive data (password hash, phone number) in the payload, or using a short, guessable secret.

Interview tip: Add the trade-off: easy to scale (no session store) but hard to revoke before it expires.

questions.question: JWT or session cookies: what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Sessions keep login state on the server and are easy to revoke; JWTs keep it in a signed token and are easy to scale but hard to revoke.

How it works:
Sessions: the browser holds only a random id; the server looks it up in Redis or a database on each request. Logout or "block user" works instantly. All servers need the shared store.
JWT: no lookup needed to trust the token, works well for mobile apps and many services. But a stolen token works until it expires, and tokens are larger.
A common mix: short-lived JWT access tokens plus refresh tokens stored server-side.

Example: A banking app with "log out all devices" leans on sessions or short tokens; a public API used by mobile apps leans on JWTs.

Common mistake: Saying JWTs are "more secure" than sessions; they are a different trade-off, not more secure.

Interview tip: Pick one for a given scenario and justify it; interviewers value the reasoning more than the choice.

questions.question: Where should a web app store the auth token: localStorage or a cookie?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie is the safer default; localStorage is simpler but exposes the token to any XSS bug.

How it works: localStorage: any script on the page can read it, so one XSS bug (a bad npm package, an unescaped comment) lets an attacker steal the token and use it from anywhere. HttpOnly cookie: JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it, but the browser sends it automatically, so you must stop CSRF with SameSite=Lax or Strict (and CSRF tokens for older cases).

Example: Many SPAs keep a short-lived access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie, getting the benefits of both.

Common mistake: Choosing localStorage and then ignoring XSS, or choosing cookies and forgetting SameSite and CORS credentials settings.

Interview tip: Name both attacks (XSS and CSRF) and which storage each one affects; that is the whole answer in one sentence.

questions.question: How do you set up CORS correctly in an Express API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Allow only your real frontend origins, and if you use cookies, enable credentials and never use *.

How it works: CORS headers tell browsers which other origins may read your API's responses. For non-simple requests (JSON body, Authorization header) the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight, which must succeed. With credentials: true, Access-Control-Allow-Origin must be an exact origin, not *.

Example: AskedIn allows https://askedin.vercel.app in production and http://localhost:5173 in development, read from an environment variable.

Common mistake: Thinking CORS protects the API. It only controls what browsers allow; curl and Postman ignore it, so authentication is still required.

Interview tip: Explain the preflight request; it is behind most "CORS error" questions.

questions.question: How do refresh tokens work, and why use them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A short-lived access token is used on every request, and a long-lived refresh token, stored safely and saved on the server, is used only to get new access tokens.

How it works: The access token lives about 15 minutes, so a stolen one is useful only briefly. The refresh token (days or weeks) lives in an HttpOnly cookie and is stored, hashed, in the database. /auth/refresh checks it and issues a new access token. With rotation, each refresh also issues a new refresh token and deletes the old one. If an old refresh token is ever used again, it was stolen: revoke all the user's tokens. Logout deletes the refresh token.

Example: A user's laptop is stolen; the user clicks "log out all devices", which deletes every stored refresh token. The thief's access token stops working within 15 minutes.

Common mistake: Making the access token long-lived "because refresh is complicated", or storing refresh tokens in localStorage.

Interview tip: Say "rotation with reuse detection"; it is the phrase that shows depth.

questions.question: How do you log a user out of every device or kill old JWTs after a password change?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Store a value on the user that old tokens cannot match, and check it on every request: a passwordChangedAt time or a tokenVersion number.

How it works:
passwordChangedAt: when verifying, reject tokens whose iat (issued at) is earlier than that time.
tokenVersion: put the user's current version in the token; increase it on "log out everywhere", so every older token fails.
Both need one user lookup per request, which most APIs already do to load req.user.

Example: This project sets passwordChangedAt on reset, so a stolen token stops working as soon as the real owner resets the password.

Common mistake: Keeping a huge blocklist of every logged-out token, which grows forever.

Interview tip: Mention that this is how you get session-like control while keeping JWTs.

questions.question: What is NoSQL injection, and how do you prevent it in a Node + MongoDB API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It is sending query operators instead of plain values, so the database runs a different query than the developer intended.

How it works: Express parses JSON bodies into objects, so req.body.email can be { "$ne": null } instead of a string. Passed straight into findOne({ email }), it means "any user with an email". Prevention: validate types with a schema, convert with String(), enable mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter', true), and never build queries from raw req.body.

Example: A login that also checks the password in the query (findOne({ email, password })) can be bypassed with { "$ne": null } in both fields, logging the attacker in as the first user, often the admin.

Common mistake: Thinking MongoDB is safe from injection because it does not use SQL.

Interview tip: Show the payload and the one-line fix; concrete beats abstract here.

questions.question: Which security measures would you add to a production Express API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Several layers: secure headers, rate limits, size limits, strict CORS, validation, safe secrets and safe error messages.

How it works:
helmet: secure HTTP headers
Rate limiting: strict on login, register and password reset
Body size limit: express.json({ limit: '100kb' })
CORS: an allow-list of origins
Validation: a schema on every input, unknown fields removed
Secrets: environment variables, rotated if leaked
Errors: generic messages, no stack traces in production
Passwords: bcrypt; tokens with expiry
Dependencies: npm audit in CI
HTTPS everywhere, and logging of failed logins

Example: AskedIn uses helmet, a rate limiter that trusts the Render proxy's IP header, body size limits and a CORS allow-list.

Common mistake: Adding helmet and calling the API "secure"; one layer is never enough.

Interview tip: Use the phrase "defence in depth" and pick three measures to explain properly rather than listing twenty.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS, and what does TLS protect?
questions.answer:
Short answer: HTTPS is HTTP sent through an encrypted TLS connection. TLS encrypts the data, proves the server's identity with a certificate, and detects any change to the data on the way. Plain HTTP sends everything, including passwords and cookies, as readable text.

How it works:
Encryption: nobody on the Wi-Fi or the network path can read the request or response
Authentication: the certificate, signed by a trusted authority, proves you are talking to the real domain
Integrity: a changed byte breaks the check, so data cannot be modified silently
Handshake: client and server agree on keys first (asymmetric), then use fast symmetric encryption
Default ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443

Example: A user logs in on public café Wi-Fi. With HTTP, anyone sniffing the network sees the password; with HTTPS they see only encrypted bytes and the domain name.

Common mistake: Thinking HTTPS hides everything. The domain (SNI) and IP address are still visible, and HTTPS does not protect against bugs like SQL or NoSQL injection.

Interview tip: Mention the practical side: Render and Vercel give free certificates, set secure cookies, and add HSTS so browsers always use HTTPS.

questions.question: Which of these should you use to store passwords?
questions.answer:
Why C: bcrypt is one-way, salted and slow on purpose, which makes stolen hashes hard to crack.

Why not A: base64 is an encoding; anyone can decode it instantly.

Why not B: md5 is far too fast and broken; billions of guesses per second are possible.

Why not D: JSON.stringify just stores the password as plain text.

questions.question: Can anyone read the data inside a JWT's payload?
questions.answer:
Why B: The payload is just base64url text; paste a token into jwt.io and you can read it.

Why not A: Standard JWTs are signed, not encrypted (encrypted JWTs, JWE, are a different thing).

Why not C: Only the server can create a valid signature, but anyone can read the payload.

Why not D: Expiry does not change who can read it.

Fix: Keep secrets and personal data out of the payload.

questions.question: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript in the page from reading the cookie?
questions.answer:
Why C: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, so an XSS script cannot steal it.

Why not A: Secure only sends the cookie over HTTPS.

Why not B: SameSite controls when the cookie is sent with cross-site requests (CSRF).

Why not D: Max-Age sets how long the cookie lives.

questions.question: What is the best defence against attackers guessing passwords on your login route?
questions.answer:
Why B: Limiting attempts per IP and per account makes guessing thousands of passwords impractical.

Why not A: Token expiry has nothing to do with guessing passwords.

Why not C: GET puts the password in the URL and logs, which is worse.

Why not D: CORS only affects browsers; attack scripts ignore it.

questions.question: The login query is User.findOne({ email: req.body.email }) and an attacker sends {"email": {"$ne": null}}. What can happen?
options: It can match the first user in the database
Nothing, Mongoose blocks it by default
questions.correctAnswer: It can match the first user in the database
questions.answer:
Why B: { $ne: null } means "email is not null", which matches any user, so the first one is returned.

Why not A: It is a valid MongoDB query, so there is no error.

Why not C: sanitizeFilter is off by default; you must enable it or validate input.

Why not D: Nothing validates the body unless you add validation.

Fix: Validate that email is a string and enable mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter', true).

questions.question: Why is a JWT hard to cancel before it expires?
options: It is stored in the database
The server checks only the signature, not a stored session
questions.correctAnswer: The server checks only the signature, not a stored session
questions.answer:
Why B: A valid signature is enough for jwt.verify; nothing on the server marks a token as cancelled.

Why not A: Plain JWTs are not stored server-side; that is exactly why they are hard to revoke.

Why not C: Browser caching is not the issue; the server would accept the token from anywhere.

Why not D: JWTs normally do have an exp claim.

Fix: Check passwordChangedAt or a tokenVersion, or use short access tokens with refresh tokens.

questions.question: What is the difference between operational errors and programmer errors?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Operational errors are expected problems in a correct program; programmer errors are bugs.

How it works: Operational: invalid input, a missing record, a duplicate email, a database timeout, a failed payment. Handle them and return the right status code. Programmer: reading a property of undefined, calling a missing function, a wrong argument type. You cannot safely handle them at run time; log them, fix the code, and let the process restart if needed.

Example: A user enters a wrong password (operational, 401). A refactor leaves order.customer undefined (programmer error, 500 plus a bug fix).

Common mistake: Wrapping everything in try/catch and returning 400 for bugs, which hides them from monitoring.

Interview tip: This distinction decides what goes in the error handler's "safe message" path versus the "log and alert" path.

questions.question: How do you handle errors from async route handlers in Express 4 and Express 5?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express 4 does not catch rejected promises, so you need try/catch or a wrapper. Express 5 sends them to the error middleware automatically.

How it works: In Express 4, an async handler that throws produces an unhandled rejection: the request hangs and the error middleware never runs. The common fix was an asyncHandler wrapper that adds .catch(next). Express 5 does this itself, so handlers can just throw or await.

Example: Moving an API to Express 5 lets you delete every asyncHandler(...) wrapper and every try/catch that only called next(err).

Common mistake: Writing try/catch in every route that only does res.status(500).json(...), duplicating error logic.

Interview tip: Know both; many companies still run Express 4.

questions.question: How do you build a central error handler with a custom error class?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create an AppError with a status code, throw it from controllers, and let one error middleware turn every error into the same JSON shape.

How it works: AppError marks expected errors (isOperational) and carries the status. The error middleware shows their message to the client; for anything else it logs the full error and sends a generic 500 message. It can also map library errors: a Mongoose CastError (bad id) to 400, a duplicate key error (code 11000) to 409.

Example: Every endpoint in the API returns { success: false, message, errors? } for failures, so the frontend has one place to show error toasts.

Common mistake: Leaking internal error messages, such as a MongoDB connection string in a stack trace.

Interview tip: Mention mapping of library errors (CastError, 11000); it shows real API experience.

questions.question: What should you do with uncaughtException and unhandledRejection?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Treat them as a last safety net: log the error with full details, then exit with a non-zero code and let a process manager restart the app.

How it works: After an uncaught exception, the app may be half-way through something (an open transaction, a broken connection), so continuing is risky. Recent Node versions already crash on unhandled rejections by default. The platform (PM2, Docker, Kubernetes, Render) restarts the process within seconds.

Example: A bug throws inside a setTimeout callback; the handler logs it to the error tracker with the stack, exits, and Render starts a fresh instance.

Common mistake: Adding process.on('uncaughtException', () => {}) to "keep the server alive"; the app keeps running in a broken state and hides the bug.

Interview tip: Say "log, exit, restart" and mention a graceful shutdown attempt before exiting if possible.

questions.question: How should a Node.js API do logging in production?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use a structured logger that writes JSON with a level, a timestamp and context such as a request id, and send logs to a log service.

How it works: pino or winston instead of console.log: levels (error, warn, info, debug) let you change detail per environment; JSON lines can be searched and filtered ("all errors for userId 42"); a request id ties every line of one request together. Log each request's method, path, status and duration.

Example: A user reports "checkout failed at 3:15"; searching the logs for their user id shows the payment provider timed out on that request.

Common mistake: Logging passwords, tokens, full card numbers or whole request bodies, which turns logs into a security risk.

Interview tip: Mention log levels per environment and redacting secrets.

questions.question: What is the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end tests for an API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Unit tests check one function alone, integration tests check several parts together (route + middleware + database), and end-to-end tests check the whole app like a real user.

How it works:
Unit: fast, many of them, dependencies faked; e.g. a price or discount calculator
Integration: Supertest calls a route, which runs middleware and a test database
End-to-end: Playwright opens the real frontend and clicks through signup
The testing pyramid: many unit, a good number of integration, a few end-to-end

Example: For a login feature: a unit test for the password rules, an integration test for POST /auth/login with right and wrong passwords, and one E2E test for the whole login form.

Common mistake: Writing only E2E tests; they are slow and flaky, and when they fail it is hard to see why.

Interview tip: For backend roles, stress integration tests: they catch most real bugs in APIs.

questions.question: How do you test an Express API with Jest and Supertest?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Export the Express app without calling listen(), then use Supertest to send real HTTP requests to it in memory and check the status and body.

How it works: app.js creates and exports the app; server.js imports it and calls listen(). Tests import app.js, so no port is opened and tests can run in parallel. Use a separate test database (or mongodb-memory-server), clear it before each test, and seed only what each test needs.

Example: A test registers a user, logs in, saves the token, and then checks that GET /api/admin/users returns 403 for that normal user.

Common mistake: Running tests against the development or production database, or sharing state between tests so they pass or fail depending on order.

Interview tip: Mention that integration tests with a real (test) database give more confidence than mocking Mongoose.

questions.question: What should you mock in API tests, and what should you not mock?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Mock things outside your system that are slow, cost money or send real messages; do not mock your own database layer in integration tests.

How it works:
Mock: email (Brevo, SendGrid), payment gateways, SMS, third-party APIs, the clock when testing expiry.
Do not mock: your own Mongoose queries in integration tests, because then the test no longer checks the real query, indexes or validation.
Too many mocks give tests that pass while production breaks.

Example: The register test mocks sendEmail and checks it was called with the user's address, but uses a real test database to check the user was saved with a hashed password.

Common mistake: Mocking User.findOne to return a fake user, then shipping a query with a typo in the field name that the test never noticed.

Interview tip: Use jest.useFakeTimers() or a mocked Date for token-expiry tests; it is a good concrete example.

questions.question: How do you debug a Node.js application?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Locally, run Node with --inspect and use breakpoints in Chrome DevTools or VS Code. In production, use logs, CPU profiles and heap snapshots.

How it works: --inspect opens a debugging port; --inspect-brk also pauses on the first line (useful for scripts). In DevTools (chrome://inspect) or the VS Code debugger you can set breakpoints, step through code and inspect variables. node --watch restarts on file changes. For production: structured logs with request ids, --cpu-prof for slow code, heap snapshots for memory.

Example: A seed script fails halfway; running it with --inspect-brk and a breakpoint in the loop shows one record has a missing topic.

Common mistake: Debugging only with console.log in production and redeploying for every new log line.

Interview tip: Mention conditional breakpoints and the VS Code "auto attach" setting; it shows daily practice.
questions.codeSnippet:
node --inspect server.js
node --inspect-brk scripts/seed.js
node --cpu-prof server.js   # writes a .cpuprofile to open in DevTools

questions.question: Memory keeps growing in production until the app restarts. How do you find the cause?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Confirm the growth with metrics, then take heap snapshots some time apart and compare which objects keep increasing.

How it works: 1) Watch process.memoryUsage().heapUsed over hours; a sawtooth that keeps rising is a leak.
2) Take 2-3 heap snapshots (DevTools, or v8.writeHeapSnapshot() on a signal) under load.
3) Use the comparison view to see which constructors grow.
4) Follow the retainers to the code that holds them.
Usual suspects: a Map or cache without a limit, arrays that collect data per request, listeners or timers never removed, closures holding big objects.

Example: Snapshots show thousands of growing strings retained by a Map called rateLimitHits; the in-memory rate limiter never removed old IPs.

Common mistake: Raising the memory limit or adding a daily restart and calling it fixed.

Interview tip: Mention comparing snapshots, not reading one; a single snapshot rarely shows a leak.

questions.question: Which of these is a programmer error, not an operational error?
options: A user sends an invalid email
questions.answer:
Why C: It is a bug in the code; the fix is changing the code, not handling it at run time.

Why not A, B and D: These are expected situations a correct program must handle with a proper response or retry.

questions.question: In Express 4, an async handler throws and there is no try/catch. What happens?
options: The request hangs and an unhandled rejection is reported
The error is ignored and 200 is sent
questions.correctAnswer: The request hangs and an unhandled rejection is reported
questions.answer:
Why B: Express 4 does not look at the promise a handler returns, so the rejection is unhandled and no response is sent.

Why not A and C: That is Express 5's behaviour, not Express 4's.

Why not D: Nothing sends a response, so the client gets nothing, not 200.

Fix: Use an asyncHandler wrapper or try/catch with next(err), or upgrade to Express 5.

questions.question: What should a process do after an 'uncaughtException'?
options: Log it and exit, so a process manager restarts it
questions.correctAnswer: Log it and exit, so a process manager restarts it
questions.answer:
Why B: The app's state may be broken, so the safe move is to log it and restart cleanly.

Why not A: Continuing in an unknown state can corrupt data and hides the bug.

Why not C: There is no general way to know which request caused it or that retrying is safe.

Why not D: Clearing a cache does not fix a broken state.

questions.question: Why export the Express app from app.js without calling listen() there?
options: So tests can use it with Supertest without opening a port
questions.correctAnswer: So tests can use it with Supertest without opening a port
questions.answer:
Why B: Tests import app.js and send requests in memory; server.js calls listen() for real runs.

Why not A: listen() is not deprecated.

Why not C: It does not change speed at run time.

Why not D: Express works either way; it is a testing convention.

questions.question: Which tool lets tests run against MongoDB without installing a database server?
questions.answer:
Why B: It downloads and starts a real MongoDB binary in memory for the test run.

Why not A: jest.fn() creates mock functions, not a database.

Why not C: nodemon restarts the app on file changes.

Why not D: supertest sends HTTP requests; it does not provide a database.

questions.question: Which flag starts Node so Chrome DevTools or VS Code can attach a debugger?
questions.answer:
Why B: --inspect opens the debugging port (9229 by default); --inspect-brk also pauses on the first line.

Why not A: There is no general --trace flag for debugging (there are specific ones like --trace-warnings).

Why not C: --prof writes a low-level V8 profiling log, not a debugger connection.

Why not D: --debug-mode does not exist.

questions.question: Why does Node.js have child processes and worker threads if it is single-threaded?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Because CPU-heavy work blocks the single JavaScript thread. Worker threads, child processes and cluster let Node use more cores and keep the main thread free.

How it works:
worker_threads: run JavaScript in parallel threads inside the same process
child_process: run another program or Node script as a separate process
cluster: run several copies of your server process to use every CPU core
The main thread stays responsive for requests while the heavy work happens elsewhere.

Example: An app generates PDF invoices: a worker thread builds the PDF, so the API keeps answering other users during the 2 seconds it takes.

Common mistake: Using these for I/O work such as database calls; I/O is already non-blocking, so it only adds overhead.

Interview tip: Start with "single-threaded for JavaScript, not for the machine" and then map each tool to its use.

questions.question: What is the difference between spawn, exec, execFile and fork?
questions.answer:
Short answer: spawn streams a command's output, exec buffers it through a shell, execFile runs a program without a shell, and fork starts another Node script with a message channel.

How it works:
spawn: streams stdout/stderr; good for long or large-output commands (ffmpeg)
exec: runs in a shell and buffers all output (1 MB limit by default); handy for short commands, risky with user input
execFile: like exec but without a shell; safer and a little faster
fork: a special spawn for Node scripts with process.send() and the 'message' event

Example: A video app uses spawn('ffmpeg', [...]) and reads progress from stderr; a deploy script uses execFile('git', ['rev-parse', 'HEAD']) to get the commit hash.

Common mistake: Using exec for a command that prints a lot, which fails with "maxBuffer exceeded", or passing user input to exec.

Interview tip: Explain "shell or no shell"; it is the security part interviewers look for.

questions.question: What are worker threads, and when should you use them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Worker threads run JavaScript in parallel inside the same process, each with its own event loop and memory. Use them for CPU-bound work.

How it works: A worker is started with new Worker(file, { workerData }). It talks to the main thread with postMessage; data is copied, or transferred without copying for ArrayBuffers, and SharedArrayBuffer allows real shared memory. Good uses: hashing big files, image processing, parsing very large JSON, heavy calculations.

Example: An image-upload API resizes photos in a worker pool, so a 300 ms resize does not delay other users' requests.

Common mistake: Moving database queries or HTTP calls into workers; they are already async, so you just pay for an extra V8 instance.

Interview tip: Say "CPU-bound goes to workers, I/O-bound stays on the event loop".

questions.question: What does the cluster module do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: cluster starts several worker processes from one primary process; all of them share the same port, so the app can use every CPU core.

How it works: The primary forks workers (often one per core). Incoming connections are spread across workers, round-robin on most systems. Each worker is a full copy of the app with its own memory and event loop. If one crashes, the others keep serving and the primary can start a replacement.

Example: On an 8-core server, one process uses one core; with cluster, 8 workers handle about 8 times the CPU-bound traffic.

Common mistake: Expecting workers to share variables, sessions or in-memory caches; each worker has its own memory.

Interview tip: Mention that in containers you often run one process per container and scale replicas instead.

questions.question: Worker threads, cluster or child processes: how do you choose?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Worker threads for a heavy calculation inside a request, cluster to run more copies of the whole server, child processes to run another program or isolate risky work.

How it works:
Worker threads: cheap data exchange, optional shared memory; e.g. resizing an image
Cluster: scale the web server across cores and survive crashes; e.g. a busy API on one big machine
Child process: run ffmpeg, Python, git or ImageMagick, or keep untrusted work in a separate process

Example: A video platform uses cluster (or replicas) for its API, a worker pool for thumbnail generation, and spawn('ffmpeg') for transcoding.

Common mistake: Reaching for cluster to fix one slow, CPU-heavy route; every worker would still block on that route.

Interview tip: Give the three one-liners; it is a classic comparison question.

questions.question: Why is exec with user input dangerous, and what should you use instead?
questions.answer:
Short answer: exec runs the command through a shell, so user input can add extra commands (command injection). Use execFile or spawn with an argument array, and validate the input.

How it works: In a shell, characters such as ; && | and $( ) start new commands. If a query parameter is pasted into the command string, "photo.jpg; rm -rf /" runs two commands. execFile and spawn pass arguments directly to the program without a shell, so those characters are just text.

Example: An image converter route builds exec(`convert ${req.query.file} out.png`); an attacker downloads the server's .env file with a crafted file name.

Common mistake: "Escaping" input by hand with replace() and calling it safe.

Interview tip: Combine both fixes: no shell (execFile) plus an allow-list or strict pattern for the input.

questions.question: Write a worker thread example that does heavy work without blocking requests.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Put the heavy code in a worker file that reads workerData and posts the result back, then wrap the worker in a promise and await it in the route.

How it works: The worker gets its input through workerData and replies with parentPort.postMessage. The route creates the worker, resolves on 'message', rejects on 'error' (and on a non-zero 'exit'). While the worker computes, the main event loop keeps serving other requests.

Example: GET /fib/40 takes about a second of CPU. In the main thread it freezes the API; in a worker the API keeps responding.

Common mistake: Creating a new worker on every request in production; use a pool (see the next question).

Interview tip: Show the promise wrapper; it is what makes workers easy to use with async/await.

questions.question: After moving to cluster mode, users get logged out at random. Why?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Each worker has its own memory, so sessions stored in memory exist in only one worker; the next request may go to another worker that does not know the user.

How it works: The same applies to in-memory caches, rate-limit counters and WebSocket rooms. Fix: keep shared state outside the process (Redis or the database), or use stateless JWTs. For WebSockets, use sticky sessions plus an adapter such as the Socket.IO Redis adapter so messages reach users on other workers.

Example: Rate limiting also breaks: with 4 workers, each counts separately, so a user gets 4 times the allowed attempts. A Redis store for the rate limiter fixes it.

Common mistake: Turning on sticky sessions for everything to hide the problem; the state is still lost when a worker restarts.

Interview tip: Say "the app must be stateless to scale horizontally"; that is the principle behind the answer.

questions.question: Why should you not create a new worker thread for every request?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Starting a worker creates a new V8 instance, which costs tens of milliseconds and several MB of memory; under load this can cost more than the work itself.

How it works: Use a fixed pool of workers, usually sized to the CPU cores, and send tasks to it. Pool workers stay warm, so each task starts immediately, and the pool queues tasks when all workers are busy, which also protects the server from overload. Libraries such as piscina do this for you.

Example: 100 parallel uploads each start a worker: the server creates 100 V8 instances, memory jumps by hundreds of MB and the container is killed. With a pool of 4, tasks queue and memory stays flat.

Common mistake: Making the pool bigger than the number of cores; the extra workers just compete for the same CPUs.

Interview tip: Mention queue limits and timeouts for the pool; they show production thinking.

questions.question: How do PM2 cluster mode and Docker/Kubernetes replicas relate to Node's cluster module?
questions.answer:
Short answer: PM2's cluster mode is Node's cluster module plus process management. In containers you usually run one process per container and scale by adding replicas.

How it works: pm2 start app.js -i max forks one process per core using cluster, restarts crashed ones, keeps logs and supports zero-downtime reloads. Docker and Kubernetes take over those jobs at a higher level: each container runs one Node process, the orchestrator restarts it, and a load balancer spreads traffic across replicas. Either way the app must be stateless.

Example: On a single VPS, PM2 cluster mode is the simple way to use all cores. On Kubernetes, the same app runs as 4 replicas of 1 process each.

Common mistake: Running PM2 cluster inside every Kubernetes pod as well, which doubles the layers of process management and makes resource limits confusing.

Interview tip: Show you know where each tool fits: VPS -> PM2, containers -> replicas.
questions.codeSnippet:
pm2 start server.js -i max     # one process per core
pm2 reload server              # zero-downtime restart

questions.question: Which module runs JavaScript in parallel threads inside one Node process?
questions.answer:
Why C: worker_threads creates threads inside the same process.

Why not A: cluster creates separate processes.

Why not B: child_process also creates separate processes.

Why not D: events is the EventEmitter module; it has nothing to do with threads.

questions.question: Which child_process function runs a command through a shell and buffers all of its output?
questions.answer:
Why B: exec uses a shell and returns the whole output at once (1 MB limit by default).

Why not A: spawn streams the output and does not use a shell by default.

Why not C: fork starts a Node script with a message channel.

Why not D: execFile buffers output but runs the program without a shell.

questions.question: How does the cluster module help a Node web server?
options: It makes each request use more threads
It runs several processes that share one port, so all CPU cores are used
questions.correctAnswer: It runs several processes that share one port, so all CPU cores are used
questions.answer:
Why B: Each worker is a full copy of the server, and connections are spread across them.

Why not A: A single request still runs on one thread in one worker.

Why not C: cluster does no caching.

Why not D: Every worker still has its own normal event loop.

questions.question: What is fork() mainly used for?
options: Starting another Node.js script with a message channel
questions.correctAnswer: Starting another Node.js script with a message channel
questions.answer:
Why B: fork() starts a Node script as a child process and connects them with process.send() and the 'message' event.

Why not A: Copying files is fs.copyFile.

Why not C: Threads come from worker_threads; fork creates a process.

Why not D: Restarting is done by a process manager, not fork().

questions.question: Why is exec(`convert ${req.query.file} out.png`) dangerous?
options: It allows command injection through the shell
convert does not exist on Linux
questions.correctAnswer: It allows command injection through the shell
questions.answer:
Why B: A value like 'a.jpg; rm -rf /' becomes a second shell command.

Why not A: Speed is not the issue; security is.

Why not C: ImageMagick's convert is common on Linux.

Why not D: exec runs any command, including ones that read files.

Fix: Use execFile('convert', [file, 'out.png']) and validate the file name.

questions.question: Can worker threads share memory with the main thread?
options: Yes, all variables are shared automatically
Only through SharedArrayBuffer (or by transferring objects)
questions.correctAnswer: Only through SharedArrayBuffer (or by transferring objects)
questions.answer:
Why C: Normal messages are copied. SharedArrayBuffer is truly shared, and ArrayBuffers can be transferred (moved) without copying.

Why not A: SharedArrayBuffer does allow shared memory.

Why not B: Each worker has its own heap; normal variables are never shared.

Why not D: Cluster workers are separate processes and share no memory at all.

questions.question: Why should you not use synchronous fs functions inside request handlers?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Sync functions block the event loop until the disk finishes, so every other user waits.

How it works: readFileSync, writeFileSync and the other Sync functions stop the single JavaScript thread. A 20 ms read on each request means the server can handle at most about 50 requests per second, no matter how many cores it has. They are fine at startup (reading a config file once) and in CLI scripts.

Example: A route that serves a template with fs.readFileSync works in development, but under load response times climb for every route.

Common mistake: Thinking a small file is always fast; on a busy or network disk, a "small" read can take much longer.

Interview tip: Say where Sync is acceptable (startup, scripts) to show you are not following the rule blindly.

questions.question: How does Redis caching speed up an API? Explain the cache-aside pattern.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Cache-aside: check Redis first; on a hit return the cached value, on a miss read from the database, save the result in Redis with an expiry, then return it.

How it works: Redis keeps data in memory, so reads take under a millisecond compared with several milliseconds or more for a database query. Cache-aside keeps the application in control: the cache is filled only with data someone asked for, and a TTL makes old entries expire by themselves.

Example: The AskedIn languages list is read on almost every page and changes rarely; caching it for 5 minutes removes most of those database queries.

Common mistake: Caching user-specific or permission-dependent data under a shared key, so one user sees another user's data.

Interview tip: Mention hit rate and TTL, and that you would cache only hot, rarely changing data.

questions.question: What is cache invalidation, and which strategies do you know?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Invalidation means removing or refreshing cached data when the real data changes, so users do not see old values.

How it works:
TTL only: simple, but data can be stale until it expires
Delete on write: remove the key whenever the data changes; accurate, but every write path must remember it
Versioned keys: languages:v42, bump the version on update
Write-through: update the cache at the same time as the database
Most APIs combine a short TTL with delete-on-write as a safety net.

Example: An admin activates JavaScript; the update route deletes the 'languages' key, so the next visitor sees JavaScript immediately instead of after 5 minutes.

Common mistake: Forgetting one write path (a bulk upload or a script) that changes data without clearing the cache.

Interview tip: Quote the classic joke ("two hard things: cache invalidation and naming things") and then show you know real strategies.

questions.question: What is database connection pooling, and how should a Node app connect to MongoDB?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A pool keeps several database connections open and reuses them. Connect once at startup and share that connection everywhere.

How it works: Opening a connection (TCP + TLS + authentication) takes tens of milliseconds, so doing it per request is slow and can exhaust the database's connection limit. The MongoDB driver keeps a pool (maxPoolSize, 100 by default); Mongoose uses it automatically after mongoose.connect(). Size it for your server and for the database plan's limits.

Example: A serverless function that connects on every call quickly hits Atlas's connection limit; caching the connection outside the handler fixes it.

Common mistake: Calling mongoose.connect inside a route or middleware.

Interview tip: Mention that with cluster or many replicas, the total is pool size times processes, which must stay under the database limit.

questions.question: How should you handle configuration and secrets across environments?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read all config from environment variables, keep a git-ignored .env file only for local development, set real values in the hosting platform, and validate them at startup.

How it works: dotenv or node --env-file loads .env locally; Render, Vercel or Kubernetes secrets provide values in production. Validate required variables at startup and stop with a clear message if one is missing, instead of failing later on a random request. Set NODE_ENV=production so libraries switch to production behaviour. Rotate any secret that leaks.

Example: AskedIn's server needs MONGO_URI, JWT_SECRET and the Brevo key; locally they come from server/.env, on Render from the service's environment settings.

Common mistake: Committing .env to git, or putting secrets in frontend environment variables (anything with VITE_ is public in the browser).

Interview tip: Mention startup validation; it turns a confusing runtime bug into a clear deploy error.

questions.question: How do you reduce API response size and time?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Send only what is needed, in pages, compressed, and let clients cache what rarely changes.

How it works:
Projection: select only the fields the screen uses
Pagination: never return unbounded lists
Compression: gzip or brotli via middleware or a proxy such as Nginx
.lean(): plain objects from Mongoose for read-only data, which is faster
HTTP caching: Cache-Control and ETag for data that rarely changes

Example: A users list sent full documents (bookmarks, hashes, history) at 2 MB; selecting name, email and createdAt with a limit of 20 made it 8 KB.

Common mistake: Removing fields in JavaScript after loading full documents; the database and network already did the expensive work.

Interview tip: Measure first (response size, time to first byte) and mention which change gave the biggest win.

questions.question: How do you shut down a Node server gracefully?
questions.answer:
Short answer: On SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests finish, close database connections, then exit, with a timeout as a safety net.

How it works: Platforms send SIGTERM before stopping a container and SIGKILL after a grace period (often 30 seconds). server.close() stops new connections and calls back when open ones finish; then close MongoDB and Redis and exit. A timer forces exit if something hangs. For long keep-alive connections, server.closeIdleConnections() helps.

Example: Without it, each deploy cuts off users mid-checkout; with it, deploys are invisible to users.

Common mistake: Calling process.exit(0) directly in the SIGTERM handler, which kills requests that are still running.

Interview tip: Mention health checks: mark the instance unhealthy first so the load balancer stops sending new traffic.

questions.question: After a release, API p95 latency jumped from 100 ms to 2 s. How do you investigate?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Find out what changed and where the time goes: all endpoints or one, CPU or waiting, then profile or check queries. Roll back first if users are badly affected.

How it works: 1) Compare the release diff and the timing of the jump.
2) All endpoints slow: suspect the event loop (lag, CPU) or a shared dependency (database, Redis).
3) One endpoint slow: check its queries; explain() for missing indexes, N+1 queries, too much data loaded.
4) Check outgoing calls: a slow third-party API without a timeout.
5) Profile with --cpu-prof or Clinic.js Flame.
6) Fix, add a test or alert, and write a short postmortem.

Example: The release added a filter on status; explain() shows a full collection scan, and an index on { user: 1, status: 1 } brings p95 back to 90 ms.

Common mistake: Guessing and redeploying random changes instead of measuring.

Interview tip: Structure the answer as a process (scope, hypothesis, measure, fix, prevent); that is what the interviewer is grading.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it in a Node + MongoDB API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: You run 1 query for a list and then 1 more query for each item. It is fast with test data and very slow in production.

How it works: For 20 posts with authors, that is 21 queries, each with network latency. Fix it by loading related data in one go: Mongoose populate (which batches with $in), one find with $in on the collected ids, an aggregation with $lookup, or DataLoader in GraphQL.

Example: A dashboard showing 50 orders with customer names made 51 queries and took 800 ms; one $in query brought it to 40 ms.

Common mistake: Hiding N+1 inside a helper (getAuthorName(id)) called in a loop, so it does not look like a query.

Interview tip: Mention logging the query count per request (mongoose.set('debug', true) locally) to catch it early.

questions.question: Why does a Node app crash with "JavaScript heap out of memory", and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The V8 heap has a size limit; loading too much data at once (or a leak) goes past it. The real fix is streaming or batching, not only a bigger limit.

How it works: The default limit depends on the system and Node version (often around 2-4 GB on 64-bit, lower in small containers). A big file read, a huge query result, or building a giant array or string can exceed it. --max-old-space-size raises the limit, but it must stay below the container's memory or the OS kills the process instead.

Example: A monthly report loads 500,000 orders with find() and crashes a 512 MB Render instance; a Mongoose cursor that writes rows to a CSV stream uses about 60 MB.

Common mistake: Raising --max-old-space-size above the container's memory, which turns a clear Node error into a mysterious OOM kill.

Interview tip: Separate the two causes: too much data at once (stream it) versus a leak (heap snapshots).

questions.question: What is a message broker like Kafka or RabbitMQ, and when does a Node.js API need one?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A message broker sits between services: producers publish messages and consumers process them later, at their own speed. It decouples services, absorbs traffic spikes and allows retries. Kafka is a durable, replayable log built for very high throughput; RabbitMQ is a classic queue with flexible routing and per-message acknowledgements.

How it works:
Producer: the API publishes an event like "order.created" and responds to the user at once
Broker: stores the message safely until someone reads it
Consumer: a worker sends the email, updates stock or generates a PDF
Kafka: messages stay in a log for days, many consumer groups can read and replay them
RabbitMQ: a message goes to a queue and is removed after a consumer acknowledges it

Example: On checkout the API saves the order and publishes "order.created". The email, inventory and analytics services each consume it separately, so a slow email server never slows the checkout.

Common mistake: Adding Kafka to a small app. A simple job queue such as BullMQ on Redis is enough until you have many services or huge volume.

Interview tip: Talk about failure handling: retries, dead-letter queues and making consumers idempotent because a message can arrive twice.

questions.question: Design a feature that shows how many visitors are online on a website right now.
questions.answer:
Short answer: First define "online", for example "seen in the last 60 seconds". Each open page sends a small heartbeat (or keeps a WebSocket open). The server stores each visitor's last-seen time in a Redis sorted set, counts the entries newer than 60 seconds, removes older ones, and pushes or serves that count to the pages.

How it works:
Visitor id: a random id in localStorage (or the user id when logged in), so one person with many tabs counts once
Heartbeat: every 20-30 seconds, or use the WebSocket connection itself
Store: ZADD online <now> <visitorId> in Redis; it is fast and shared by all Node instances
Count: ZCOUNT online <now-60s> +inf, and clean up with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE online -inf <now-60s>
Show: broadcast the count over WebSocket/SSE every few seconds, or let pages poll a cached endpoint
Scale: never write every heartbeat to MongoDB; Redis handles it, and the number can be slightly approximate

Example: A news site has three Node servers behind a load balancer. All of them write heartbeats to the same Redis sorted set, and one timer broadcasts "1,245 people reading now" every 5 seconds.

Common mistake: Counting open sockets on a single server (wrong with many servers), or never removing visitors who closed the tab.

Interview tip: Start with the questions an interviewer expects: exact or approximate? per page or whole site? how many users? Then size the design to the answers.

questions.question: Which signal do Docker and Kubernetes send first when they stop your app?
questions.answer:
Why B: SIGTERM politely asks the app to stop, giving it time to shut down gracefully.

Why not A: SIGKILL comes after the grace period and cannot be caught.

Why not C: SIGINT is what Ctrl+C sends in a terminal.

Why not D: SIGHUP traditionally means the terminal closed or config should reload.

questions.question: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?
options: Read from the database, save it in the cache, then return it
Wait until the cache is filled
questions.correctAnswer: Read from the database, save it in the cache, then return it
questions.answer:
Why B: The application loads the data itself and fills the cache so the next request is a hit.

Why not A: The user would get wrong data.

Why not C: Nothing else fills the cache in cache-aside; the app must do it.

Why not D: Clearing everything would make every request a miss.

questions.question: Where should mongoose.connect() be called?
questions.answer:
Why B: One connect at startup creates the pool that every request then reuses.

Why not A: Connecting per request is slow and can exhaust database connections.

Why not C: Models use the shared connection; they should not connect themselves.

Why not D: Connecting after requests makes no sense; the connection must exist before them.

questions.question: What reduces the size of large JSON responses sent over the network?
options: Compressing responses with gzip or brotli
questions.correctAnswer: Compressing responses with gzip or brotli
questions.answer:
Why B: JSON is repetitive text, so gzip or brotli often shrink it to a small fraction of its size.

Why not A: The method does not change the response size.

Why not C: Middleware by itself does not shrink anything (except compression middleware).

Why not D: Sending twice is an error, not an optimisation.

questions.question: Listing 20 orders with their customers runs 21 database queries. What is this called?
questions.answer:
Why B: 1 query for the list plus 1 per item: the N+1 problem.

Why not A: A race condition is about timing between concurrent operations.

Why not C: A deadlock is when operations wait on each other forever.

Why not D: A cache stampede is many requests rebuilding the same expired cache key at once.

Fix: Load the customers with one $in query or populate.

questions.question: A Node app in a 512 MB container crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory" while building a big report. What is the best first fix?
options: Stream or paginate the data instead of loading it all into memory
questions.correctAnswer: Stream or paginate the data instead of loading it all into memory
questions.answer:
Why B: Processing one batch at a time keeps memory flat, whatever the report size.

Why not A: The process runs out of memory, not time.

Why not C: CPU cores do not add heap memory.

Why not D: var vs const has no effect on memory use.
